items.r: A block is only closed at its content_block_stop, and the turn is only confirmed at message_stop: acting on the deltas means acting on partial JSON strings, which can only be parsed once the block closes. The failure you have to recognise is exactly this one: a tool use error on a retry that traces to a half-built block, not to the schema or to a version change.

items.q: A stream cuts out in the middle of a tool_use block. What can you NOT do?
o: Accumulate the partial deltas and reconstruct the call.
Resume the response from the last fully complete text block.
Discard the turn and fire the whole request again.
Log the cut and warn the user about the failure.
items.r: The docs are explicit: tool use and reasoning blocks cannot be partially recovered. You can only resume from the last text block, and discarding or logging the cut is always available. It is the most tempting distractor because technically you are holding the bytes.

items.q: You are going to ingest document scans at 3000×2000 px. What do you do before writing the ingestion code?
o: Upload them via the Files API, which does not consume any input tokens.
Compute the visual tokens: ⌈width/28⌉ × ⌈height/28⌉.
Convert them all to greyscale to bring the per-image token cost down.
Pick the cheapest model available for that ingestion workload.
items.r: Claude sees 28×28 px patches, and the formula has to be run against the largest input expected in production, not against the test set. The image is rescaled automatically if it exceeds the tier limit. Greyscale does not change the number of patches, and the Files API avoids resending bytes on every turn but the content is still charged as input tokens.

items.q: The team says it is already doing "batching" because it fires a thousand synchronous calls in parallel from a loop. What do you correct?
o: That this is not batching: it does not lower cost per token.
Nothing: the effect is the same when parallelism is high enough.
That it should lower parallelism to avoid hitting 429s.
That it should use streaming on each of those calls.
items.r: It is the mistake the material names explicitly: a thousand parallel synchronous calls give throughput, not a discount. The Message Batches API is the one that gives lower cost per token, in exchange for non-deterministic latency. The three routes for images each have their place: inline base64 for single use, Files API for assets reused across requests, and Batches for offline work.

items.q: You can specify the goal and the available tools, but not the path between them because it depends on what turns up along the way. Workflow or agent?
o: Agent only if volume exceeds a certain load threshold.
Agent: you fix the goal and the toolset, not the path.
Workflow, with conditional branches for every possible case.
Workflow, because it always works out cheaper to run.
items.r: The operational formulation: workflow when you can write the exact steps in code; agent when you can specify goal and tools but not the path. Volume does not enter the decision, and conditional branches only cover the cases you already know about. Getting it wrong only shows in production — a workflow where an agent was needed breaks on the first input off the path.

items.q: One of your agent's tools can issue refunds, an irreversible action. When is the human checkpoint introduced?
o: Before wiring the loop, as part of the design.
After the first production incident, with real failure data.
Only if the amount exceeds a threshold to be decided later.
Not needed if the tool records every call in an audit log.
items.r: Human-in-the-loop over irreversible actions is a design decision, not a later correction: after the first incident the write has already reached the customer's environment. And a log is forensic, not preventive.

items.q: Your agent works in testing with long, continuous sessions, but in production the sessions turn out to be short and very numerous. You use in-context memory. What happens and what do you do?
o: Nothing: with short sessions in-context memory performs even better.
Move to summarised memory, which preserves everything at lower cost.
Move to stateless and rebuild the context on every request.
It fails: the state has to move to external storage.
items.r: In-context memory is the pattern that fails first with that session shape: what was learned dies with each short session. State must move to external storage, accepting latency in exchange for surviving between sessions. Scope is decided by the shape of the session, not by how easy it is to implement. Summarised memory does not "preserve everything": it loses whatever the summariser's prompt did not preserve. And stateless only works for jobs that complete and close.

items.q: You want the same review procedure applied across different tasks without pasting it into every session. State or instructions?
o: Instructions: duplicate them in each project's CLAUDE.md.
Repeatable instructions: that is a Skill, not memory.
State: store it in the agent's external memory.
State: inject it into every session's system prompt.
items.r: Carrying state and carrying repeatable instructions are different problems. State is memory; the reusable procedure is a Skill: a markdown file loaded on demand when its description matches the task. That is precisely its advantage over injecting it into every system prompt or duplicating it in each CLAUDE.md.

items.q: The pipeline runs security reviews on about 50 PRs a day at $150/day with the synchronous API. The reviews do not block: devs merge when the tests pass and address the findings afterwards. The Batch API is being evaluated for its 50% saving. Which factor determines whether batch is appropriate?
o: Whether cutting latency per review from 30-60 s to near-instant matters for the flow.
Whether feedback arriving up to 24 h after the PR is created is still actionable.
Whether processing can handle reviews arriving in a different order from the one sent.
Whether each review can be structured as a single request with no multi-turn refinement.
items.r: The Batch API processes asynchronously with a window of up to 24 h. The only thing that decides suitability is tolerance of that latency, and since the reviews do not block, it fits. Cutting latency is the opposite of what batch does; ordering is solved with custom_id; and being single-shot is true but is not what decides.

items.q: A dev refactors a function with Claude Code and, before committing, asks the same session to review the code. Afterwards, an independent CI review finds several bugs the in-session review missed. What best explains the discrepancy?
o: Claude retains the context of its own prior reasoning in the session.
The CI review uses a more specific prompt for catching subtle bugs.
The CI environment sees the whole codebase, the local session only the file.
The extended session filled the context window with conversational history.
items.r: It is self-review bias: retaining the prior reasoning makes it less likely to question its own decisions, so it validates its assumptions rather than attacking them. The CI review starts in a clean context, having decided nothing; it does not win by having a better prompt or more files. Derived practice: review your own code in a fresh session or subagent, not in the same thread.

items.q: Each PR is reviewed with a single API call and a static prompt containing the diff and the modified files; unmodified files are not included. The reviews are asynchronous. Cross-file interaction bugs slip through systematically (a PR renames parameters and does not flag the callers in untouched files). They account for 35% of incidents. Most effective change?
o: Run per-modified-file passes including their direct dependents, and aggregate and deduplicate with a final call.
Add chain-of-thought asking it to list every external reference in the diff and reason about how it affects the callers.
Use static analysis to build a dependency graph and include every file within two hops of any modified file.
Redesign the review as an agentic task with a turn limit, where the model reads and searches the codebase with tools.
items.r: The problem is context access, not reasoning: the model cannot flag callers it never sees. The agentic loop follows references to verify cross-file findings and retrieves only what it needs; being asynchronous leaves ample latency headroom. Two hops of dependency bloats the context and adds noise; CoT reasons better about absent information, which is to say it speculates; and the static passes still see no further than the direct dependents.

items.q: The review produces many findings, but devs dismiss half of them as "not worth addressing". Analysis shows the dismissed ones are technically correct but concern minor style preferences or patterns acceptable in that codebase. Before adding infrastructure, which prompt change most reduces the dismissals?
o: Add explicit criteria defining what to report (bugs, security) and what to omit (minor style).
Instruct it to report only findings it is highly confident are genuine problems.
Implement a secondary classifier that filters findings by predicted dev acceptance.
Ask it to score each finding's confidence from 1 to 10 and include only those scoring 8 or above.
items.r: The dismissals are not technical false positives: they are correct but irrelevant findings. The problem is defining relevance, not confidence, and the explicit criteria must also cover the patterns that are acceptable in that codebase. "Only if you are very sure" raises the certainty threshold, not the importance threshold, and suppresses subtle bugs. Self-assessed confidence measures technical certainty, not value to the team. And the classifier is the infrastructure the question asks you to avoid.

items.q: The review uses tool_use with a report_findings tool that returns a JSON array of findings. On large PRs of more than 30 files the response hits max_tokens and the JSON is truncated, breaking the parser. Most effective way to handle it?
o: Raise max_tokens to the model maximum and instruct that descriptions stay under 50 words.
Detect the truncated JSON and resend asking only for critical and high severity.
Split the review into several calls, each over a subset of files.
Stop using tool_use and ask for the findings as a markdown list.
items.r: The root cause is that output volume scales with PR size. Only splitting removes it structurally: each call has bounded output, the finding arrays are merged afterwards and it scales to any size, and it allows parallelism too. Markdown still truncates and loses structure on top; the retry is reactive and discards valid medium findings; and raising the ceiling does not remove it.

items.q: The review misses real bugs. The prompt includes: "Flag only critical problems that would definitely cause production failures. Ignore minor concerns and anything you are not sure about." Devs confirm there are logic errors the model investigated and decided not to report. The team requires structured, labelled output. Which change removes the suppression while preserving the metadata?
o: Enable extended thinking and instruct it to reason step by step about each change before producing the review.
Remove all the severity instructions and let the model use its default judgement.
Add a second pass rereading the diff with the same prompt looking for what was omitted.
Instruct it to report every finding with a confidence level and severity, filtering later.
items.r: The cause is that the prompt asks for suppression at generation time, and information is lost there irrecoverably. Deferring the filtering to a later step preserves everything, and the confidence and severity labels are exactly the metadata the team requires. Extended thinking improves the reasoning but the suppression instruction remains; removing all the instructions also removes the metadata; and a second pass with the same prompt repeats the error.

items.q: The review systematically flags patterns the team uses deliberately: force-unwrapping in tests, large coordinator classes that follow the established architecture, and internal imports marked deprecated. 30% of the findings are dismissed. What stops the model from generating them, supplying the conventions as persistent context on every review?
o: Add inline suppression comments and preprocess the diffs to exclude those lines.
Build post-processing keyword filters that suppress findings with terms like "force unwrap" or "deprecated import".
Analyse only the changed lines of the diff, with no surrounding context.
Document the accepted patterns and intentional conventions in the project's CLAUDE.md.
items.r: The question asks for persistent context on every review, and CLAUDE.md is exactly that mechanism in Claude Code. The model stops generating those findings because it knows they are deliberate decisions. Suppression comments clutter the code and stripping lines from the diff loses real bugs; cutting context increases false positives by convention; and keyword filtering also suppresses the cases where the pattern really is a problem.

items.q: Test generation produces unit tests for new code, but 55% are low value: trivial assertions that only check nothing throws, duplication of existing coverage, or disregard for the fixture conventions. How do you reduce that rate at source?
o: Document testing standards in CLAUDE.md: criteria for a valuable test and available fixtures.
Two-phase generation, with a second call that scores each test and filters out low scores.
Add post-generation coverage analysis that filters out tests which do not increase line coverage.
Restrict generation to the directories with the highest historical acceptance rate.
items.r: The ask is to reduce generation "at source". The three observed failures are context deficits and CLAUDE.md covers them in one go: criteria for what makes a test valuable, available fixtures with their use case, and examples distinguishing meaningful tests from trivial assertions. The coverage filter acts afterwards and is a poor proxy besides: a trivial test can add lines and a good edge-case one may add none. The second phase is also post-generation and doubles the cost. Restricting directories does not improve quality, it just gives up.

items.q: A step classifies and summarises 200 commits at the end of each weekly release, with one call per commit to the Messages API on Sonnet. The notes are not needed until the next morning (12 h of headroom). Cost per token must come down while keeping the model and the prompts. Which approach meets every constraint?
o: Send the 200 requests to the Batch API with unique custom_ids and collect the results when they finish.
Concatenate the 200 messages into a single request, since fewer requests reduces total token cost.
Fire the 200 requests in parallel over concurrent connections, since concurrency lowers the price per token.
Switch from Sonnet to Haiku to take advantage of its lower per-token rates on input and output.
items.r: The Batch API meets all three at once: a 50% discount on input and output, it keeps the model and the prompts, and 12 h fits comfortably inside the 24 h window. Concurrency affects throughput, not price per token: false premise. Changing tier is explicitly forbidden. And "fewer requests reduces the cost" is also false: you pay for tokens, not per request, and it changes the prompt too.

items.q: CI jobs take 18 s to initialise before analysing code. Profiling points to the auto-discovery of hooks, MCP servers, plugins, skills and several nested CLAUDE.md files in the monorepo. Startup must be cut while keeping the team standards, which live in the root CLAUDE.md.
o: Run in --bare and specify all the review criteria in the -p argument of each invocation.
Run in --bare and pass --append-system-prompt-file ./CLAUDE.md with the team standards.
Replace the prompt with --system-prompt-file ./CLAUDE.md, which skips the default assembly.
Keep the default initialisation and add a flag to exclude dynamic sections from the system prompt.
items.r: There are two requirements and only one option meets both: --bare removes the auto-discovery that causes the 18 s, and --append reinjects the one file needed at trivial cost, without dropping the standards. Replacing the whole prompt throws away Claude Code's base capabilities for reviewing code. Putting the criteria in -p works but duplicates the standards in the CI script and drifts out of sync. And keeping the default initialisation keeps the cause of the delay.

items.q: A single prompt covers security, API design and business logic correctness. Recall is 82% on API design and 34% on logic edge cases. Adding few-shot examples of logic bugs raises logic to 41% and drops API design to 68%. How do you address the trade-off?
o: Replace the few-shot examples with a detailed checklist of specific logic edge cases.
Split into separate focused prompts: one for security and API design, another for business logic.
Move up to a more capable model tier, whose reasoning will handle both in a single prompt.
Supply the entire repository as context instead of only the changed files.
items.r: The trade-off is the evidence: raising one category lowers the other, which is to say competition for attention within the same prompt. As long as they share a prompt, any gain in one is paid for in the other; splitting into focused prompts, each with its own examples, removes the competition, and the findings are consolidated before the review is published. A better model raises both numbers but the competition remains, and it is a tier change, not a design change. More context adds noise. And the checklist swaps one focus mechanism for another inside the same single prompt.

items.q: The pipeline invokes claude -p --system-prompt "$PROMPT" passing the diff on stdin. The reviews complete, but Claude only comments on the diff text: it never reads repository files, not even when the diff modifies a function called from many modules. Which change makes it read related files while still applying your instructions?
o: Keep --system-prompt and add --allowedTools "Read,Glob,Grep", which -p mode disables by default.
Embed the diff inside the prompt string instead of passing it on stdin, so it becomes an agentic session.
Remove --system-prompt and put the instructions in a CLAUDE.md, since --system-prompt is incompatible with tools under -p.
Replace --system-prompt with --append-system-prompt, so the instructions add to the default prompt.
items.r: --system-prompt replaces the base prompt entirely, and with it the built-in guidance on how and when to use Read, Glob and Grep to navigate the repository. The tools are still available, but the model no longer has instructions to use them. --append keeps that guidance and adds your criteria on top. Moving the diff to another channel changes nothing; --system-prompt being incompatible with tool use is a false premise; and -p does not disable the tools.

items.q: Reviews of PRs with more than 50 files take over 20 minutes and cost between $8 and $12 per run, because of long agentic loops. The team needs each invocation to abort on reaching a fixed number of iterations and a fixed dollar amount, enforced by Claude Code and not by the job runner.
o: Set timeout-minutes: 5 on the GitHub Actions step and monitor the cost on the Console dashboard.
Set --permission-mode dontAsk to automatically deny unlisted permissions.
Change --model to a smaller one so each iteration uses fewer tokens.
Add --max-turns 10 --max-budget-usd 2.00 to the claude -p invocation.
items.r: Two specific caps enforced by Claude Code are asked for. --max-turns cuts the agentic loop and --max-budget-usd aborts on reaching the spend, with a clean cut too: Claude finishes and returns what it has instead of having its process killed. The timeout is enforced by the job runner, exactly what is ruled out, and the dashboard only observes after the fact. A smaller model makes each iteration cheaper but does not limit how many there are. And permissions are neither iterations nor budget.

items.q: 35% of the findings are false positives with consistent patterns: style suggestions that contradict the conventions, security warnings about patterns that are safe in their deployment context, and performance suggestions that would degrade their use case. What best lets the model generalise its judgement to new code patterns?
o: Add instructions like "be conservative", "flag only definite problems" and "consider that some patterns may be intentional".
Implement post-processing with keyword matching to filter findings.
Include few-shot examples with annotated snippets distinguishing acceptable patterns from genuine problems in each category.
Create an exhaustive specification of every pattern that must not be flagged and include it in full in the system prompt.
items.r: Generalisation to new patterns is what is asked for, and there examples beat rules: an annotated example conveys the underlying judgement and the model extrapolates it. Vague calibration instructions raise the threshold indiscriminately and teach no judgement. An exhaustive list is enumeration, not generalisation: by definition it does not cover what you have not seen, and it inflates the prompt. Keyword filtering is brittle and does not generalise.

items.q: The organisation has enabled managed Code Review via the Claude GitHub App. It averages 18 findings per PR with three kinds of noise: style the linter already enforces in CI, findings on autogenerated code in src/gen/, and auxiliary rendering patterns that are intentional conventions. Only 4 per PR are real bugs. Most effective way to reduce the noise?
o: Create a REVIEW.md at the root with omission rules and a verification requirement for the rendering findings.
Configure separate GitHub Actions workflows per code area, with suppression on the generated code and dedicated prompts on rendering.
Add custom instructions with the action's prompt parameter, with one rule for each kind of noise.
Add explanations to the project's CLAUDE.md about which patterns are intentional and that linting is handled separately.
items.r: The key detail is that this is the review managed by the GitHub App, not an action in your own CI. That service is tuned with files in the repository: REVIEW.md, at the root, holds instructions for reviews alone, and it is where you say what not to report (what CI already enforces, generated paths such as src/gen/) and where to require evidence before a finding is posted, which is what rendering calls for: a higher bar, not suppression. CLAUDE.md is read too, but as project context: it makes violations of its rules get flagged, it does not exclude paths or categories. The prompt parameter and separate workflows belong to the action you run in your CI, which is a different product and does not configure the managed review.
items.c: REVIEW.md: instructions for reviews alone. Use it to say what your team wants flagged, at what severity, and what to skip.

items.q: The extraction system has had 100% human review for 3 months. Extractions with confidence ≥90% have 97% overall precision and the intent is to automate them. Before deploying, what is the most critical validation step?
o: Compare precision at different thresholds (85%, 90%, 95%) to find the optimal cut-off.
Verify that the 97% precision meets the requirements of every downstream system.
Pilot for two weeks routing 25% of the high-confidence ones downstream and monitor errors.
Analyse precision by document type and by field, not only in aggregate.
items.r: 97% is an average and averages hide pockets of failure: there may be a document type or a field at 80% masked by the rest, and automating on the aggregate leaves those errors systematically unreviewed. Breaking it down by segment verifies that performance is consistent, and it is the validation you can do before deploying, because three months of data already exist. Optimising the threshold comes later; checking downstream also starts from the aggregate; and the pilot detects the problem in production already.

items.q: Event details must be extracted from calendar invitations and returned as JSON strictly conforming to a schema. Downstream systems reject malformed or non-conforming JSON. Which approach gives the most reliable conformance?
o: Include detailed formatting instructions and the schema in the prompt, and parse the text response.
Prefill the response with an opening brace to force JSON, then complete and parse the text.
Define a tool whose input schema is the target schema and have Claude invoke it.
Instruct "return only valid JSON matching the schema exactly" and re-ask when parsing fails.
items.r: Tool use enforces the schema at API level, not as a suggestion in the prompt: when the tool is invoked with the extracted data, the input field of the tool_use block arrives already as a structured, validated object, with no text to parse and no risk of preamble, markdown or trailing commas. Instructions are advisory; the prefill forces the start but not the structure of the rest; and retrying is reactive and does not cover JSON that parses fine but breaks the schema.

items.q: The schema has property_type as an enum of four values. After deployment, 8% fail validation: the listings mention studio, loft, duplex, mobile home, tiny house, converted warehouse, and new types keep appearing regularly. Most effective long-term solution?
o: Add few-shot examples showing how to map unexpected types to the closest enum value.
Continuously extend the enum with newly observed types and add failure monitoring.
Add an "other" value to the enum with a property_type_detail string field for the detail.
Change property_type from enum to free string and implement normalisation in post-processing.
items.r: If new types appear regularly, any closed list fails sooner or later. "other" gives a permanent escape valve: the schema stops breaking, downstream still receives a bounded enum for the common cases, and property_type_detail preserves the literal when "other" is selected. The free string removes the failure but destroys the structural guarantee. Mapping "converted warehouse" to "house" falsifies the extraction. And extending the enum is perpetual maintenance: each new type is a production failure.

items.q: tool_use is used with a 12-field schema, around 2,500 tokens of definition. Below 150K tokens of document, accuracy is 98%. Between 175K and 190K it drops to 71% and information from the final third is systematically omitted. The window is 200K. Most likely cause?
o: Very long documents exceed the model's effective attention span regardless of context limits.
Schemas with more than 8-10 fields raise decision complexity and reduce accuracy regardless of length.
Tool definitions consume input context; added to the document, the total approaches the limit.
The model distributes attention proportionally, leaving unfocused those fields mentioned only once near the end.
items.r: The arithmetic says it: 190K of document plus 2,500 of tool definition plus the system prompt plus the room reserved for the output leaves you pressed against 200K, and what degrades is the processing of the end. It fits the pattern: the drop appears exactly in the 175-190K band and affects the final third. Attention span is plausible but does not explain an abrupt jump from 98% to 71% in a specific band; proportional attention is not the mechanism; and the first option asserts independence from length, which is the opposite of the evidence.

items.q: Extractions with confidence below 85% are routed to review. An audit reveals that 12% of the high-confidence ones also contain errors: plausible but incorrect values, from varied sources (competitor comparison tables, appendices from other variants, ambiguous phrasing). You need to catch them and measure whether improvements reduce the rate over time.
o: A verification pass that re-extracts every high-confidence document and flags discrepancies between attempts.
Heuristic rules that flag documents with comparison tables or appendices, whatever the confidence.
Stratified random sampling, reviewing a fixed percentage of high-confidence extractions weekly.
Lower the threshold from 85% to 70%, routing more volume to human review.
items.r: Two things are asked: catch the errors and measure the trend. Only stratified sampling gives instrumentation: a representative, stable sample produces a metric comparable week to week, and being random it captures error sources you do not yet know about. The review cost is also fixed. Re-extracting reproduces the same plausible errors and produces no metric; heuristics cover only the known; and lowering the threshold does not touch errors sitting above 85%.

items.q: The pipeline occasionally receives responses that do not parse as valid JSON, breaking downstream processing. Today the JSON is requested in the response text and parsed. Most reliable approach to guarantee valid, conformant structured data?
o: Define a tool with a JSON schema and use tool_use to constrain the output to conformant JSON.
Explicit formatting instructions with examples, stressing that only valid JSON should be returned with no surrounding text.
A retry loop that catches parse errors and asks again with the error details.
Regular expressions to locate and extract the JSON from the response text.
items.r: Tool use imposes the structure at the API level: the input arrives already as a validated object, with no text to parse, no preamble and no markdown. The rest are mitigations on an inherently unreliable text channel: the retry burns calls and does not cover JSON that parses but violates the schema; formatting instructions are suggestions, and that is exactly what is already failing; and regex over LLM output accepts anything shaped like braces without validating it.

items.q: 12% of extractions contain semantic errors that pass schema validation, for example a duration "30 minutes" placed in an ingredient quantity field. Reviewers can only check 20%. What best allocates their attention?
o: Prioritise extractions where required fields are empty or marked as not found.
Have the model emit field-level confidence scores and calibrate the thresholds.
Review every extraction from documents with formatting or unusual layout anomalies.
Randomly sample 20%, using the corrections to track overall accuracy.
items.r: The ask is to allocate limited capacity where it pays most. Per-field confidence points straight at the semantic error — the model shows less certainty exactly when it puts "30 minutes" into a quantity field — and calibrating the thresholds against a labelled validation set turns that signal into a measured cut-off, not a guessed one. Empty fields are a different, already visible failure; random sampling measures well but as a policy it captures only 20% with no prioritisation; and formatting anomalies correlate poorly with semantic errors.

items.q: Invoice extraction uses tool use with strict schemas. There are never syntax errors, but 12% fail semantic validation: line items do not add up to the total, or supplier IDs do not meet the format. Today they go to manual review. What reduces the volume while maintaining accuracy?
o: When validation fails, resend the document, the extraction and the errors so the model corrects it.
Post-processing that automatically corrects common errors, such as recalculating the total.
Retry up to 3 times and accept the first result that passes semantic validation.
Add stricter schema constraints with detailed descriptions on every field.
items.r: The validation error is precise diagnostic information, and handing it back to the model alongside the document and its own extraction lets the failure be located, usually a misread digit or an omitted line item. It is targeted correction and it maintains accuracy because it looks at the source again. Retrying without saying what failed repeats the error, and "the first one that passes" rewards whatever slips through. Stricter schemas do not prevent semantic errors. And recalculating the total fabricates data: if a line item was omitted, you generate an incorrect total that now passes validation.

items.q: After implementing tool use with strict schemas the syntax errors disappear, but 5% have valid JSON with empty arrays or nulls in required fields such as citations and methodology. The documents do contain the information, in varied formats: inline citations versus bibliographies, methodology sections versus details embedded in introductions.
o: Make citations and methodology optional and flag incomplete records for manual review.
A post-processing layer with regex that scans for citation patterns and methodology keywords.
Add few-shot examples of extractions over varied document structures and formats.
Retry logic that resends the request when validation detects empty required fields.
items.r: The information exists; the model does not recognise it when it appears in a format it does not expect. That is a pattern-recognition deficit and annotated examples are the direct mechanism: they demonstrate how to identify citations in different formats and where to locate methodology by section type, and they teach that a bibliography and an inline citation are the same entity. It also generalises to new formats. Making the fields optional hides the failure; regex over varied formats is where it works worst; and retrying with the same prompt reproduces the same failure.

items.q: Event metadata is extracted from press articles with every field nullable. The model frequently generates plausible but incorrect values for fields that are not mentioned: it returns "500" for attendee_count when the source says nothing about attendance. Most effective way to reduce this?
o: Make every field required and apply strict validation rules on each one.
A post-processing second call that verifies each extracted value exists in the document.
Instruct it to return null for any field not stated directly in the source.
Move up to a more capable model tier, with better schema instruction following.
items.r: The schema already allows nulls, but the model does not know that "absent" is an acceptable answer: it assumes it must fill every field, which is why it invents a plausible "500". Instructing it explicitly gives it permission to abstain, at no additional per-call cost. A better model reduces the problem at the margin but the ambiguity remains; downstream verification detects rather than prevents and doubles the cost; and making every field mandatory forces invention precisely when the data does not exist.

items.q: Two document types are processed with the same schema: standard monthly reports that are archived once processed, and urgent exception reports that must trigger alerts within 30 minutes. Cost must be minimised while meeting the latency. How do you architect the pipeline?
o: Queue everything and send hourly batches, flagging the urgent ones for expedited handling on return.
Route the standard ones to the Batch API for the 50% saving and the urgent ones to the Messages API in real time.
Send everything to the Messages API in real time to guarantee consistent latency.
Send everything to the Batch API with custom_id and, when the results arrive, process the urgent ones immediately.
items.r: The two types have different latency requirements, so differentiated routing is the correct architecture: the monthly ones are archived and take the discount, the urgent ones have a 30-minute SLA that the Batch API does not guarantee. Putting the urgent ones in a batch does not work even if they are processed "immediately on arrival", because they can take hours. Hourly batches do not bound total latency. And real time meets the SLA but pays full price for all the monthly ones.

items.q: The pipeline uses an extract_metadata tool and also lookup_citations and verify_doi for enrichment. With requests like "extract the metadata and tell me how cited it is", Claude sometimes calls lookup_citations first, which fails because it needs the DOI that extract_metadata would provide. Most effective way to ensure the order?
o: Set tool_choice to "any" and prioritise extract_metadata in the pipeline's system prompt.
Set tool_choice to extract_metadata and handle the enrichment in later turns.
Set tool_choice to the specific extract_metadata tool on every call in the pipeline.
Set tool_choice to "auto" and reorder the tools array so extract_metadata appears first.
items.r: Forcing the specific tool guarantees the first turn always extracts metadata, and leaving the enrichment to later turns is what completes the answer: the dependency resolves because lookup_citations is invoked once the DOI is already in context. Forcing it on every call stops the enrichment from ever running. "any" forces the use of some tool, not a specific one. And the order in the tools array does not determine selection priority: false premise.

items.q: After a daily batch of 10,000 documents completes, 300 (3%) fail with context_length_exceeded. The results file identifies each failure by custom_id. Most cost-effective approach?
o: Resubmit the whole batch with a model tier with a larger context window.
Reprocess the whole batch with prompt caching enabled to make the prefix cheaper.
Resubmit only the 300 failures split into smaller pieces and combine the extractions.
Increase max_tokens for the 300 failures and resubmit them in a new batch the next day.
items.r: The error is that the document does not fit: splitting it is the only thing that attacks that, and the custom_ids allow reprocessing only the 3%, combining the partial extractions afterwards. max_tokens limits the output, not the input, so it has nothing to do with the error. Reprocessing the 9,700 that already worked is waste and a larger tier may not be enough. And prompt caching makes the repeated prefix cheaper but does not change the fact that the document does not fit.

items.q: The schema includes skills: string[]. In production three problems appear: compound phrases like "Python and SQL" are sometimes kept together and sometimes split; implicit skills that were never stated appear; and similar documents produce arrays of 5-10 versus 40+ entries. The prompt says "Extract all skills mentioned".
o: Post-extraction normalisation that maps to a canonical taxonomy and deduplicates entries.
Enrich the schema to {skill, confidence, source_quote}[] to capture more metadata.
Add few-shot examples demonstrating compound phrases, mention criteria and granularity.
Add constraints: "extract at most 10-20 skills, one per entry, only those named explicitly".
items.r: The three problems are variations of the same thing: the prompt defines neither per-entry granularity, nor the threshold for "mentioned", nor the scope. Examples solve all three at once — how to treat "Python and SQL", what counts as an explicit mention and how much detail per entry — and convey judgement, not a rigid rule. Downstream normalisation partly fixes granularity but does not eliminate the invented skills or the length variance. An arbitrary numeric cap truncates rich documents or pads poor ones. And more metadata helps diagnose afterwards, but does not change what is extracted.

items.q: Product descriptions are parsed to extract specifications. Despite the schema, the materials field comes out inconsistent: sometimes "cotton blend", other times "Cotton/Polyester mix", and occasionally it is omitted when the information is clearly present. Most effective way to improve consistency?
o: Make the materials field required instead of optional to force a value every time.
Add 2-3 input-output pairs with the material format already normalised.
Set temperature to 0 to eliminate randomness in the extraction.
Switch to a more capable model tier, since the inconsistency indicates low capability.
items.r: The schema defines the field type, but not how to format the value nor when the information counts as present. Examples cover that gap: they fix the convention with standardised material description formats and show cases where the material appears in different ways, which also reduces the omissions. Making the field mandatory eliminates omissions but forces invention and does not touch the format. Temperature 0 reduces variance across runs on the same input, and here the inconsistency is across documents. And it is not a capability failure: it finds the information, it does not know how to normalise it.

items.q: Follow-up queries like "summarise what we have learned about market trends" take more than 40 s. The coordinator spawns the synthesis subagent on every request, passing it more than 80K tokens of accumulated findings that it already holds in its own context from having orchestrated the research.
o: Pre-generate and cache summaries at several granularities whenever new findings accumulate.
Enable prompt caching on the synthesis subagent to avoid re-transferring the same findings.
Spawn the subagent with reduced context and have it request specific findings from the coordinator.
Have the coordinator serve simple summary requests directly using its existing context.
items.r: The coordinator already holds the 80K in context: delegating means transferring them to another agent that starts from zero, and that is where the 40 seconds go. Serving them itself and reserving the spawn for complex analysis removes the entire cause. Caching makes reprocessing the prefix cheaper but you still pay transfer and start-up; requesting on demand adds a round trip and can end up slower; and pre-generating summaries nobody asks for burns compute constantly.

items.q: The research phase takes longer than expected: the coordinator invokes the web search subagent, waits, and then invokes the document analysis one and waits again. The tasks are independent. How do you run them concurrently?
o: Add instructions to the system prompt explaining the benefits of parallelism and asking it to invoke both at once.
Create an external asynchronous orchestration layer that launches parallel threads, each with a coordinator-subagent pair.
Structure the coordinator to emit both Task tool calls in a single response message.
Switch both subagents to a Haiku tier, since if each one takes less the total drops too.
items.r: That is how parallelism works in the Agent SDK: several tool_use blocks in a single response message run concurrently, whereas one per turn forces sequence because each turn waits for its tool_result. Time goes from sum to maximum. Explaining the advantages does not change the message structure: a soft instruction for a mechanical problem. Haiku speeds up each subagent but they remain serial, so the total is still the sum. And the external layer reimplements what the SDK already does.

items.q: The synthesis agent finishes its initial pass but flags that three key questions remain unanswered because search and analysis found no relevant information. The coordinator proceeds to generate the report, producing incomplete coverage. What most improves completeness?
o: Give the synthesis agent direct access to search tools to fill the gaps on its own.
Have the report generator note which questions could not be answered in order to explain the limitations to the users.
Have the coordinator detect the gaps in the synthesis and re-delegate with targeted queries before re-invoking it.
Increase the breadth of the initial queries to search and analysis so they cover more ground.
items.r: The synthesiser is already flagging exactly what is missing and that signal is thrown away. Turning it into a refinement loop translates the gaps into specific queries to search and analysis, far more effective than the generic initial search, and it keeps the coordinator-orchestrator pattern. Noting the limitations documents the failure instead of solving it; more initial breadth is a blind attempt because the gaps are only known afterwards; and giving the synthesiser tools breaks the separation of roles.

items.q: The pipeline crashed after processing 12 of 28 documents: search had identified sources, analysis had partially extracted and synthesis had begun identifying patterns. You need to resume without repeating work or losing fidelity. What state management balances fidelity and context efficiency?
o: Have each agent persist a structured export and the coordinator load the manifest on resume, injecting each one's portion.
Persist the coordinator's full conversation log with every delegation and every response, and give it to the agents on resume.
Have each agent maintain its own state file and reload it on its own at the start of each working session.
Index every output in a shared vector store and have each agent retrieve by semantic search.
items.r: The ask is to balance fidelity and efficiency, and only the manifest does both: the structured export, saved to a known location, preserves the findings precisely and the coordinator filters so each agent's prompt receives only its portion. It also preserves the orchestration. Independent files have good fidelity but reload everything unfiltered and without coordination: nobody knows what was left half done. The full log is enormous and largely irrelevant. And semantic search is approximate retrieval: restoring state demands exactness.

items.q: The document analysis agent has a single analyze_document tool with a free-text instruction parameter. "Extract the key financial metrics" often returns narrative summaries, and "summarise the methodology" sometimes returns raw data tables. 35% of results require asking again. Most effective way to improve reliability?
o: Keep the single tool and add an analysis_type enum parameter that requires explicitly selecting the type.
Improve the tool description with examples mapping each phrasing to its correct output format.
Have the coordinator pre-classify each request and then pass already disambiguated instructions to the analysis agent.
Split the tool into purpose-specific tools: extract_data_points, summarize_content and verify_claim_against_source.
items.r: The cause is an interface with no contract: a free-text parameter leaves the output format to interpretation on every call. Explicit input/output contracts remove that structurally, because extract_data_points cannot return narrative: its schema does not allow it. Better examples reduce variance but remain guidance. Pre-classifying clarifies the intent but the tool still has no output contract. And the enum only constrains the input: the output remains untyped.

items.q: The four subagents all have access to the full set of 18 tools. In testing they frequently call tools outside their specialisation: the synthesis one attempts web searches and the report generator attempts to analyse documents. Main cause?
o: The tool definitions consume too much context window and truncate the description of the task.
The coordinator cannot track which capabilities each subagent has and so routes tasks incorrectly.
The role descriptions in the system prompts conflict with having access to tools outside that role.
Choosing among 18 tools rather than 4-5 raises decision complexity beyond reliable thresholds.
items.r: Selection degrades as the option space grows: with 18 candidates, any one with a vaguely applicable description competes, and the agent calls outside its specialisation. The solution is the corollary: give each subagent only the subset of 4-5 tools its role needs. The coordinator's routing works in the scenario; context consumption is real but no truncation is mentioned; and the role prompt and the tool access do not contradict each other, they say different things.

items.q: Specialised sources are added: a financial API agent that returns JSON with revenue and margins, a news one that returns prose, and a patents one that returns structured lists. The synthesiser converts everything to bullet points, and the financial comparisons lose their tabular clarity and the news its narrative flow. What most improves the briefing?
o: Add a conversion layer between subagents and synthesis that transforms everything into a common form.
Standardise all subagent outputs to prose summaries with inline citations.
Standardise all outputs to JSON with fields for claim, evidence, source and confidence.
Update the synthesis agent to render each content type in the format that suits it.
items.r: The problem is not that the subagents produce different formats: that diversity reflects the nature of the data and is correct. The failure is in synthesis, which flattens everything into bullets and destroys information, so it is fixed where it happens: financial data as tables, news as prose. Forcing prose destroys the tabularity: same mistake in another format. The common intermediate representation moves the loss upstream. And a claim/evidence/source schema fits metric series and narrative summaries poorly.

items.q: Sometimes contradictory findings are synthesised into a confident assertion and other times the reports are over-qualified. With "analysts estimate a 50B market (methodology varies)" and "a peer-reviewed study estimates 35B (±7B, 95% CI)", the coordinator either picks one arbitrarily or produces vagueness. Systematic approach?
o: A calibration layer that normalises all uncertainty to 0.0-1.0 scores and averages them by weight.
Structure the reports with sections distinguishing well-established findings from disputed ones.
Configure the subagents to report only the findings that exceed a high confidence threshold.
A verification subagent that passes to synthesis only claims corroborated by two independent sources.
items.r: "50B with varying methodology" and "35B ±7B with 95% CI" are not the same kind of claim, and that difference is the valuable information. Preserving the original characterisations and the methodological context in explicit sections lets the reader see the peer-reviewed estimate with its interval, the analyst one with its caveat, and why they differ. Requiring two sources discards the best-characterised finding if nobody corroborates it; filtering by confidence removes the disagreement the user needs to see; and reducing "±7B, 95% CI" to a scalar and averaging fabricates a figure no source supports.

items.q: The coordinator has AgentDefinitions configured for all four subagents. In testing it reasons correctly about when to delegate — it generates messages like "I am going to ask the search agent to find sources" — but no subagent execution ever occurs, and it continues as if it had happened. The logs show no errors. Most likely cause?
o: The AgentDefinitions are fine, but the system prompt does not list the available subagent types.
The coordinator's allowedTools configuration does not include "Task", so it cannot invoke the tool that spawns subagents.
Context isolation means the task descriptions do not arrive on their own and an explicit forwarding has to be set up first.
The coordinator's max_tokens is too low and truncates the Task tool invocation before it is emitted.
items.r: It fits the three exact symptoms: it reasons well because the AgentDefinitions are in its context, nothing executes because the tool is not available, and there are no errors because a failing call is never attempted. A tool absent from the allowed set produces no error, it produces silence. Context forwarding would matter if the subagents ran with incomplete information, and here none of them run. A truncation would leave a trace. And the scenario says it reasons correctly about who to delegate to.

items.q: When analysing legal cases that cite several precedents, the analysis subagent processes them sequentially: a case with 12 precedents takes more than 3 minutes. How do you reduce the latency while preserving the coordinator's ability to monitor and debug?
o: Allow the analysis subagent to spawn its own subagents when it hits cases with many citations.
A message queue where tasks are processed asynchronously by a pool of worker agents.
Have the coordinator spawn analysis subagents in parallel, each with a subset, and aggregate the results.
A recursive hierarchy where the agents subdivide the work further down to the granularity of a single precedent.
items.r: The precedents are independent, so splitting them and analysing them in parallel turns sum into maximum, and the second half of the question decides it: the coordinator still spawns and aggregates before synthesis, with full visibility. The queue with a pool brings in infrastructure outside the SDK and decouples execution from the coordinator, which is exactly what breaks observability. Recursion adds unnecessary depth and nested traces. And dynamic spawning creates agents the coordinator neither sees nor controls.

items.q: The synthesiser receives summarised findings and passes a consolidated summary to the report generator. The reports make factual claims without citations because the source metadata was lost during the summarisation steps. Most effective approach to ensure attribution?
o: Instruct the synthesiser to embed the inline references within the text of its summary.
Have each agent emit structured data separating the content summaries from the source metadata.
Have the generator query the search agent to relocate the sources for the claims in the final report.
Skip the summarisation and pass the full raw outputs directly to the report generator.
items.r: Attribution is lost because it is embedded in prose that is then summarised. Separating it into structured fields — URLs, document names, page numbers — makes it survive every step: the content is condensed, the references propagate intact. Passing the raw outputs preserves the sources but eliminates the synthesis and swamps the generator. Relocating after the fact is reconstruction and can return a different source from the one that supported the claim. And inline references are still prose: they fall out at the next condensation.

items.q: The coordinator gives the search subagent step-by-step instructions, with exact queries, source priorities and date filters. Three problems are observed: it reports "insufficient results" instead of trying alternatives, quality drops on emerging topics that do not fit the expected patterns, and it rarely surfaces valuable tangential sources.
o: Specify research objectives and quality criteria — breadth, source diversity, recency — instead of procedural steps.
Add fallback directives: "if the specified searches return fewer than N results, try alternative phrasings".
Remove the procedural detail entirely and delegate with simple objectives like "research X thoroughly".
A classification step where the coordinator categorises requests as well-defined or exploratory and uses different instruction styles.
items.r: The three symptoms come from the same thing: prescriptive instructions that turn the subagent into a script executor. Telling it what to achieve instead of how, letting it determine its own strategy, makes it reformulate when it fails, adapt to emerging topics and pursue tangential sources because diversity becomes an explicit criterion. A single change covers all three. The fallback patches the first with more prescription; classification keeps the rigidity where it also fails; and the opposite extreme throws away the quality criteria and leaves the subagent without knowing when enough is enough.

items.q: Search has found 25 sources (120K raw tokens), analysis has extracted insights (15K) and synthesis has produced a narrative draft (3K). The coordinator must pass context to the report generator for the final output with appropriate citations. What strategy balances completeness and efficiency?
o: Pass the full accumulated context from every previous agent, so that no source is lost.
Pass the synthesis draft along with a structured index mapping the claims to their URLs and excerpts.
Pass only the draft and have a post-processing step match claims to sources and insert the citations afterwards.
Pass a condensed summary of every stage that attributes the sources by name only.
items.r: It is the balance being asked for: the 3K draft gives the narrative and the source index adds only what is needed to cite — the origin URL and the relevant excerpt for each key claim — not the 120K raw. The citations are produced during generation, not pasted on afterwards. Matching after the fact is heuristic reconstruction prone to misattribution. The accumulated 138K is waste and risks length-driven degradation. And attributing "by name only" does not allow citation: without a URL or an excerpt it cannot be located or verified.

items.q: Simple fact-checking queries run through all four subagents sequentially, consuming more than 40 s and significant tokens. Complex comparative research does benefit from the full pipeline. The query distribution is diverse and evolves as users discover new applications.
o: Train a complexity classifier on labelled historical data, retraining it periodically.
Have the coordinator analyse each query and decide dynamically which subagents to invoke based on its assessment of the requirements.
Create a fast path for factual questions that skips the subagents, routing the rest through the full pipeline.
Pattern-based routing that categorises by structure (single fact, comparative, analytical) and maps each category to a predefined combination.
items.r: The decisive detail is that the distribution is diverse and evolving: any fixed scheme — categories, rules or a trained classifier — ages with every new application. The coordinator is already a model capable of assessing requirements, and that judgement generalises to queries nobody anticipated, with no maintenance. The factual/non-factual binary is far too coarse; three predefined categories have the same problem; and the classifier demands labelling, retraining and infrastructure, and is always behind.

items.q: After the search and analysis subagents complete their tasks, the coordinator needs to spawn the synthesis one. What is the correct approach to provide it with the information it needs?
o: Include the full findings from both subagents directly in the synthesis subagent's prompt.
Provide it with tool definitions that let it request the other subagents' outputs via callbacks.
Spawn it with only a brief task description, relying on automatic context inheritance from the coordinator.
Pass reference identifiers and give it read access to a shared memory store where the others deposited their results.
items.r: Subagents in the Agent SDK have isolated context: they inherit nothing from the coordinator and cannot reach their siblings' state, so the information travels explicitly in the prompt they are spawned with. There is no shared memory store between subagents; they cannot invoke callbacks to other subagents, because communication goes through the coordinator; and automatic context inheritance is precisely the false belief.

items.q: An engineer asks you to find every caller of a function before deleting it. It is defined in a core library but also exposed through wrapper modules that rename it (calculateTax becomes computeOrderTax in the orders module). Which strategy most reliably identifies every caller?
o: Read the library and the wrappers to identify every name under which it is exposed, and Grep for each one.
Use Grep to find the files that import from the library and read each one to see if it uses it.
Search for the function name in the documentation to understand the usage patterns and the documented integration points.
Use Grep to search for the original function name across the codebase and review each match.
items.r: The problem is the renaming: searching only for calculateTax misses whoever calls computeOrderTax. Resolving the mapping first — Read over the library and the wrapper modules to discover the aliases, Grep for each name across the whole codebase — covers the full set. Correct order: discover the surface, then search for it. A legacy system's documentation is incomplete; importing the library does not imply using that function; and searching only for the original name is exactly the failure the scenario warns about.

items.q: The code review assistant analyses PRs and gives feedback on three aspects: style, security and documentation completeness. Each aspect requires reading files, running analysis and generating a section of the report. The process follows the same three-step flow for every PR. Which decomposition pattern is most appropriate?
o: Routing: classify each PR by type (feature, bugfix, refactor) and route to different prompts optimised per category.
A single exhaustive prompt with all the instructions, letting the model handle the three aspects at once.
Orchestrator-workers: have a central LLM dynamically determine which checks are needed and delegate to specialised workers.
Prompt chaining: sequential steps where each aspect is analysed separately, combining the outputs in a final synthesis step.
items.r: The key is "the same three-step flow for every PR": when the decomposition is fixed and known in advance, chaining is the correct pattern, with a focused prompt per aspect and no decision layer to pay for. Routing is for when different inputs need different treatments, and here they all get the same flow. Orchestrator-workers is designed for dynamic decompositions. And the single prompt creates competition for attention.

items.q: In exploration sessions of more than 30 minutes, the agent starts giving inconsistent answers about code structure it had already discussed, and the engineers have to repeat context about modules already explored. Most effective approach?
o: Create summaries of every source file before starting, loading only those compressed representations.
Have the agent maintain a scratchpad file with the key findings and consult it later.
Switch to a higher-capacity model tier to give more window to the accumulated data.
Automatic context clearing every 15 minutes to start with fresh context.
items.r: In long sessions the early findings end up buried under the noise of tool calls and outputs, and the model becomes unreliable about them. The scratchpad takes them out of the history and puts them in structured external storage, re-readable with precision. It solves both complaints: consistency and not repeating context. Clearing destroys exactly what needs preserving; more window delays the problem but does not avoid it, because it is signal versus noise; and pre-summarising everything is expensive, blind and does not capture what emerges during exploration.

items.q: A helper function must be inserted in the middle of a 150-line utilities module, between two existing functions. The Edit tool fails because old_string finds no unique text: there are docstrings, variable names and repetitive structural patterns. Most reliable way to complete the insertion?
o: Use Edit's replace_all targeting a common pattern, with the function embedded in the replacement.
Use Read to load the file, insert the function in place and write it back with Write.
Use Edit with an old_string of more than 30 lines of context to guarantee uniqueness.
Use Bash with a heredoc to append the definition to the end of the utilities file.
items.r: When the file offers no unique anchors, text matching is not viable, and at 150 lines Read + Write is perfectly manageable: the agent sees the full content, locates the exact position and writes the result. Deterministic and with no dependence on an unrepeatable string. A 30-line old_string is fragile and with repeated patterns it may still not be unique; the heredoc with append puts the function at the end; and replace_all substitutes every occurrence, inserting it several times.

items.q: After 25 minutes exploring a game engine's rendering subsystem, an engineer asks to understand how the physics engine integrates for the debug overlays. The recent answers are observed to talk about "typical rendering patterns" instead of the VulkanPipeline and FrameGraph classes discovered earlier. Most effective approach?
o: Use /clear to reset the context and start from scratch with the file paths from CLAUDE.md.
Spawn a subagent to explore physics independently and manually synthesise its findings.
Summarise the rendering findings and spawn a physics subagent with that summary in its context.
Continue in the current context with more targeted prompts that reference the classes by their exact name.
items.r: Answering with "typical patterns" instead of VulkanPipeline and FrameGraph indicates saturated context and diluted findings. Condensing what was learned and starting the physics exploration in clean context solves both halves. /clear throws away 25 minutes of work and CLAUDE.md gives paths, not findings. Continuing in the same context does not fix the saturation. And a subagent that does not know the rendering work cannot identify the integration, and the manual synthesis would be done from the already degraded context.

items.q: A newly joined engineer asks to understand the authentication and authorisation architecture of a codebase of more than 800 files spread across several services. Which strategy best builds understanding given the built-in tools and the context limits?
o: Spawn parallel subagents that explore different services and synthesise their findings.
Read CLAUDE.md and the READMEs first, and ask the engineer to specify the 10-15 most important files.
Use Grep to locate the authentication entry points and follow imports and calls from there.
Read every file containing auth, login, permission or token in its content or name.
items.r: It is targeted retrieval versus bulk loading: with 800+ files the agent finds the anchors with Grep, reads only those files and follows imports and calls to map the flow incrementally, and each step informs the next, which is what produces architectural understanding. Asking the new joiner to point out the key files is asking for exactly what they came to find out. Per-service subagents lose how they connect to each other. And keyword search without following references is massive noise.

items.q: After initial searches, the agent has identified that the caching logic spans 15 files — decorators, middleware and service classes — around 8,000 lines. The engineer is going to add a new invalidation trigger. Most effective next step in terms of managing context?
o: Use Read to load the 15 files one by one and build a complete understanding first.
Use Grep to search for "invalidate" and "expire" and read only those line ranges with minimal context.
Use Glob to find files with caching patterns, prioritise the largest and review the small ones afterwards.
Identify the base cache class from the imports, read its interface and trace the implementations.
items.r: They are going to add a new trigger, so they need the abstraction: what contract it must satisfy and how the existing ones implement it. Analysing imports and hierarchies to reach the base class, reading its interface and tracing the concrete invalidation implementations from there gives the mental model that organises the other 14 files and makes the tracing targeted rather than exhaustive. 8,000 lines at once saturate and produce details without architecture. Line ranges are efficient but fragmentary: you see isolated calls without the contract that governs them. And Glob by name is redundant, quite apart from size not correlating with importance.

items.q: An engineer asks you to find every file in the monorepo that imports the @company/auth package. Which built-in tool is most appropriate?
o: Glob, to find files with "auth" in the name or in the package path.
Grep, to search for the import statement pattern in file contents.
Read, starting with the package.json files to trace the dependency declarations.
Bash, with find to locate the directories that have "auth" in the name.
items.r: What is being asked lives in the content, not the name, and Grep is the content search tool with a literal, precise pattern. Searching directories by name says nothing about who imports the package. Glob searches by name and path: an orders.ts may import auth and an auth-helpers.ts may not. And the package.json files declare dependencies at package level, not which specific files import them.

items.q: A subagent has spent 30 minutes analysing a legacy payments system, with 47 files read and flows documented. The session is interrupted by a connection drop and, meanwhile, a colleague merges a PR that renames two utility functions. The engineer wants to continue the same exploration. Most effective approach?
o: Resume from the transcript without mentioning the changes: the architectural understanding remains valid.
Spawn a new subagent including the previous transcript in the initial prompt.
Spawn a new subagent with a summary of the previous findings.
Resume the subagent from its previous transcript and inform it about the renamed functions.
items.r: Resuming preserves the 30 minutes of work with no loss and no reconstruction cost, and flagging the renaming corrects the only part of the state that has gone stale. A summary loses detail relative to the full transcript and also does not mention the renaming. Resuming without flagging it carries stale references forward. And putting the transcript into a new subagent is redundant when resumption exists, and it does not correct the renaming either.

items.q: After adding an MCP server with refactoring tools (extract_function, rename_variable, inline_function), the agent still uses Write and sed in Bash. The server is connected and healthy, and each tool has a minimal description along the lines of "extract_function: extracts a function from code". Most effective way to improve adoption?
o: Accept it, since sed is more predictable than specialised refactoring tools would be.
Improve the descriptions: when to prefer each tool over editing text, plus inputs and outputs.
Remove the Write tool in refactoring sessions so it has no option left but to use the MCP ones.
A classifier that detects refactoring intent and routes automatically to the MCP server.
items.r: Selection is based on the descriptions: "extracts a function from code" does not say when to choose it over a sed, nor what it takes or returns, so when in doubt the model falls back on what it knows. Making the usage criteria and the input/output contract explicit addresses the cause. Removing Write forces by elimination, breaks legitimate writes and teaches nothing about when each tool applies. The classifier adds infrastructure and takes the decision away from the agent. And the last one is false: refactoring tools operate on the structure of the code, so they are more reliable than sed.

items.q: The agent is configured with three MCP servers: git, Jira and documentation search. Faced with "create a branch for JIRA-123 and add documentation links to the ticket", how does it access these servers' tools?
o: You must specify which server to use on each turn, and it can only access one at a time.
The agent queries each server in turn to find out which one handles each tool, routing by prefixes.
The agent automatically selects the most relevant server and loads only its tools.
The tools from every server are discovered on connection and are available at the same time.
items.r: That is how MCP works: at start-up the client issues tools/list against each server and aggregates all the definitions into a single set, which is why the agent can chain git, Jira and documentation within one task. There is no prior server selection: all the tools are loaded and the model chooses tool by tool. You do not have to indicate a server and there is no limit of one per turn. And the routing is not discovered at execution time: each tool is already associated with its server from the initial discovery.

items.q: In a security scanning flow you need to locate every occurrence of a dangerous function such as eval() in a large codebase. Which tool should the agent use for the content search?
o: Bash, running ls -R with a filter to recursively list the files containing eval.
Grep, to search for the eval( pattern across every file in the codebase.
Glob, with a pattern like **/*eval* to find files and read each match.
Read, reading the main entry file and following the imports to trace where it might be used.
items.r: Grep is the content search tool and it returns the file and line of each occurrence, which is what a security scan needs. Tracing imports from the entry point is slow, incomplete and eval does not always arrive via an import. Glob searches by name: a file called eval-utils.js is not the same as one that uses eval(). And recursive listing with a filter filters the list of names, not the content.

items.q: Engineers frequently ask to cross-reference code changes with Jira tickets during reviews: descriptions, acceptance criteria and recent comments. Today the content has to be copied and pasted manually. The team wants direct access to this standard Jira data. Most effective approach?
o: Use Bash with curl against the Jira REST API, with authentication headers and inline JSON parsing.
Export the tickets to markdown files in the repository that the agent accesses with Read.
Integrate an existing Jira MCP server that exposes tickets, comments and metadata.
Build a custom MCP server wrapping the Jira API with tools designed for the team's review flow.
items.r: The key phrase is "standard Jira ticket data", which is exactly what a standard MCP server covers: you integrate it and the agent accesses in real time with tools discovered at connection. Exporting to markdown creates copies that go stale instantly, and the recent comments would not be there. Hand-rolled curl means credentials in shell commands and manual parsing repeated on every call. And building a custom MCP is only justified if specialised tools are needed that do not exist.

items.q: An engineer sees an unfamiliar error in production logs, "SYNC_CONFLICT: entity version mismatch detected", but does not know which of the 12 services generates it. Which exploration approach most efficiently finds the responsible code?
o: Use Glob to find files in error-handling directories across all the services and read every match.
Read the README and the service configurations to understand the architecture, and then systematically read each service's files.
Use Grep to find the files that import the error-handling module and read them to locate the definitions.
Use Grep to search for distinctive text from the message and then read the matching files to understand the context.
items.r: The error message is a literal string that exists in the source: Grep locates it across the 12 services in a single pass, with maximum signal and minimum cost, and Read afterwards only on the hits. Searching by error directories assumes a structure that may not exist, because custom errors often live alongside the domain logic. Searching for who imports the module is indirect. And systematically reading 12 services is the opposite of efficient.

items.q: The agent connects to three MCP servers: issue tracker, documentation wiki and database explorer. On cross-system questions like "which tables are affected by the PROJ-1234 authentication refactor?" it makes 8-10 sequential calls, issues exploratory calls because it lacks visibility into what each server contains, and exhausts the context. Which change best exploits MCP's capabilities?
o: Consolidate the three into a unified MCP server with cross-referencing capabilities.
Add a prepare_investigation tool to each server that takes the question and returns summaries.
Add an orchestrator that routes each question to a single server based on its keywords.
Expose each server's catalogue as MCP resources: issues, documentation and schemas.
items.r: The ask is explicitly to exploit MCP's capabilities, and resources are the primitive designed for this: a discoverable content catalogue — issue summaries, documentation hierarchy, database schemas — the agent inspects without executing a tool. It attacks the root cause — lack of visibility — and therefore eliminates the exploratory calls, shortens the chain and saves context. The investigation tool puts logic in every server and is still one call per server. Routing to a single one breaks the cross-system questions. And consolidating is a costly redesign that gives up the modularity.

items.q: Claude summarises a new regulation and cites a specific subsection number. Before sending it to compliance, what do you do?
o: Send it as is: the summary sounds confident and grounded.
Ask it to score its own confidence and send it if it is high.
Rephrase it in a more formal, legal tone before sending.
Verify the citation against the official text of the rule.
items.r: Verification happens before sharing, and against the official source, not against the summary itself. Precise-looking details — article numbers, references, figures — are exactly where hallucinations appear. Self-declared confidence is not a signal of accuracy, and reformatting does not fix correctness.

items.q: In which of these cases is human review essential before using the output?
o: A summary of your own notes from an internal call.
A severance calculation communicated to affected employees.
A brainstorm of names for an internal Slack channel.
A draft agenda for a weekly team meeting that decides nothing.
items.r: The criterion is consequence and irreversibility, not difficulty. When the error affects people, money or a legal obligation, human validation stops being optional. A channel name, an agenda or a summary of your own notes are free to fix: the error is visible and undone before it causes harm.

items.q: You compare two versions of the same generated text and do not know which is better. Most solid approach?
o: Pick the longer one: it is usually more developed.
Pick the one with the most technical, precise vocabulary.
Ask Claude to choose without giving it any criteria.
Define two or three measurable criteria and score both.
items.r: Criteria are fixed before looking at the output, and they must be specific and measurable. Without a rubric up front, the comparison measures which version sounds better to you, which is not the same as which one works. Length and technical vocabulary are proxies for apparent effort, not quality; and asking Claude to choose with no criteria moves the problem rather than solving it.

items.q: You asked for an analysis and the output is correct but disorganised for your executive audience. What do you do first?
o: Iterate on the format that audience needs.
Accept it and rewrite the whole thing by hand.
Switch to another model and run the request again.
Start a new conversation and ask for it from scratch.
items.r: The content is already correct: the problem is presentation. Adapting the output to the audience is an explicit objective of the blueprint, and the cheap route is to ask for the specific structure it needs, with an example if necessary. Rewriting by hand throws away work already done; switching model or conversation does not fix a formatting defect.

items.q: You need a quarterly report that requires gathering data, analysing it, drafting and adapting the tone. A single prompt gives mediocre results. What do you apply?
o: Repeat the same prompt and keep the best attempt you get.
Move up to a more capable model without changing anything.
Decomposition: split into subtasks and validate each step.
An even longer prompt with all of the instructions at once.
