items.r: Task decomposition is objective 1.2 of the blueprint, and it matches the prompt chaining pattern: you chain subtasks, validate each step before the next, and trade some latency for accuracy. A longer prompt concentrates the same problem; repeating until it lands is a lottery with no criteria; and a better model on a badly framed task still does four things at once.

items.q: A research prompt returns generalities. Which adjustment is most likely to improve it?
o: Add "be thorough and highly professional" at the end of it.
Ask for three times the length to force more detail.
Repeat the same question using different wording.
Specify audience, scope, quality criteria and output format.
items.r: Generic outputs usually come from generic prompts. Adjectives describe an aspiration; scope, criteria and an example of what you consider a good answer define it. More length produces more generalities, not more substance, and rewording the same vague question returns the same vague answer.

items.q: Which prompting strategy best fits a brainstorming session versus an analysis one?
o: In brainstorming, volume and variety; in analysis, criteria and reasoning.
In both, demand maximum precision and one single answer from the first prompt.
In brainstorming, constrain the format tightly; in analysis, leave it open.
In both, ask for the final conclusion with no intermediate steps shown.
items.r: Adapting the strategy to the task type is objective 1.4. In ideation you diverge first — volume and variety — and filter afterwards; in analysis you anchor criteria and ask for explicit reasoning before the conclusion. Option 2 inverts the constraints: it straitjackets exactly where variety is needed. And asking for the conclusion with no steps removes the place where the error would show.

items.q: A manual 6-step process takes 4 hours a week. You are asked to "automate it with Claude". First move?
o: Replace the whole process with a single very long prompt.
Analyse the process before deciding what to automate.
Automate the 6 steps as they are, to keep the known process.
Start with the hardest step, which is where the value is.
items.r: The blueprint distinguishes integrating from redesigning. Automating a bad process produces a faster bad process: two of the six steps may be redundant and only one may deserve AI. Preserving the known process preserves its defects too; the hardest step is not necessarily the one eating the hours; and a single prompt erases the checkpoints.

items.q: An executive asks whether they can trust the contract summaries your workflow generates. Best answer?
o: Assure them the model is very accurate and almost never gets it wrong.
Say that AI should never be used for contract work at all.
Show them the usage and adoption metrics for the tool.
Explain what it does well, where it fails and the check built in.
items.r: Communicating value and limits to stakeholders is an explicit objective of domain 4: the real scope, the built-in human verification step and when it triggers. Neither overselling nor rejection. And usage metrics measure adoption, not reliability: how many people use it says nothing about whether it is right.

items.q: You are introducing Claude into an onboarding workflow that four teams touch. What do you do before rolling it out to everyone?
o: Let each team adopt it their own way, without any coordination.
Pilot with one team, measure against the current process.
Roll out to all four teams at the same time to maximise impact.
Write the full documentation up front and consider the job done.
items.r: Iterative solution design: pilot, measure against the baseline and adjust before extending. It is the same as a product rollout, and it stops a design flaw propagating to four teams at once. Documentation describes the design, it does not validate it; and uncoordinated adoption produces four different processes that cannot then be compared.

items.q: They want to upload a spreadsheet with client names and account numbers to analyse trends. Policy restricts sharing regulated personal data. What do you do?
o: Upload it as is, since the analysis is internal and stays in.
Upload it while telling Claude not to retain or use the data.
Drop the analysis: with regulated data there is no clean route.
Anonymise the identifiers before uploading and analyse that.
items.r: Anonymisation allows the trend analysis without exposing the regulated data: names and account numbers add nothing to the aggregate. Internal use does not exempt you from policy; an instruction to the model is a request, not a compliance control; and dropping it is unnecessary when a clean route exists.

items.q: Which of these is an inappropriate use case as stated?
o: Drafting job descriptions that HR will review before use.
Summarising responses from an already anonymised internal survey.
Preparing interview questions for the manager to validate.
Letting the model decide on its own who is made redundant.
items.r: The last three keep the person as the decision-maker, with review before anything takes effect. The first delegates a high-impact decision about people to a non-deterministic system, with no review and no recourse for the person affected. The problem is not that the model touches HR work, but that it decides alone.

items.q: Your organisation has no formal AI use policy yet and the team already uses Claude daily. Correct stance?
o: Apply the existing data-handling standards and escalate.
Wait for a policy to exist before using the tool for anything.
Assume that, with no policy, any use is permitted by default.
Write a policy yourself and apply it to the other teams.
items.r: The absence of a specific AI policy does not create a vacuum: the data classification and handling rules already in force still apply. Spotting the governance gap and escalating it is part of the role. Waiting blocks use that is already legitimate; a gap is not permission; and writing policy for other teams assumes authority you do not have.

items.q: You need to generate hundreds of short customer reply drafts: speed and cost take priority over deep reasoning. What do you choose?
o: Turn off product features in order to reduce the total cost.
Switch AI platform in search of lower prices per request.
A faster, cheaper model for high-volume, straightforward work.
The most capable and most expensive model for every single reply.
items.r: Match the model to the task requirements: short, repetitive drafts do not need deep reasoning. The top model on simple work burns budget and latency with no quality gain; turning off features degrades the product without touching cost per reply; and switching platform does not address the trade-off, it relocates it.

items.q: Every week you work on the same 12 reference documents and repeat the context in every chat. Which feature fits?
o: Open a new chat per document and work through them separately.
Ask Claude to remember last week's documents from memory.
A Project with those documents as its knowledge base.
Paste the documents at the start of every new conversation.
items.r: This is the canonical Projects case: persistent knowledge plus project-level instructions, instead of rebuilding the context by hand every time. Pasting the documents repeats the work every week; one chat per document breaks exactly the cross-document analysis; and context does not survive from one conversation to the next on its own.

items.q: A very long conversation starts giving incoherent answers and forgetting earlier agreements. What do you do?
o: Switch to a more capable model within the same thread, which will retain more.
Summarise the state and the key decisions and start a new thread with them.
Keep pushing with more detailed and explicit prompts in the same thread.
Ask it to reread the conversation from the beginning before answering.
items.r: This is the objective "when to restart, summarise or persist". The fuller the window gets, the worse it remembers: restarting with a dense summary restores the signal. Pushing, rereading or switching model all leave the saturated context intact, which is the cause of the problem.

items.q: A Project used to give good results and has started degrading after six months. Most likely cause?
o: The knowledge sources and the instructions have gone out of date.
The model has lost capability over time and answers worse than before.
The Project has exceeded the conversation limit it can accumulate.
Instructions are automatically deleted after a period, by design.
items.r: Maintaining and updating configurations, sources and instructions is an explicit objective of domain 5: nobody has maintained them. A Project is a living artefact: if the source documentation changes and it does not, it starts answering with the world of six months ago. The model does not degrade by itself, no conversation limit affects quality, and instructions do not expire.

items.q: What distinguishes a good system-level instruction from a bad one?
o: It is as short as possible so as not to consume context needlessly.
It lists exhaustively everything the model must never do or say.
It includes whole example conversations as a reference for style.
It defines role, scope, output format and what to do at edge cases.
items.r: A good system instruction is operational: role, limits, format and behaviour in the face of the unexpected; it does not stop at quality adjectives. "Be professional and accurate" changes none of the model's decisions. Brevity is not an end in itself, a list of prohibitions does not say what to do, and full dialogues spend context without fixing any criterion.

items.q: A prompt that worked well starts giving poor results after three new requirements are added. How do you diagnose it?
o: Add a fourth requirement asking for more care with the other three.
Switch to another model and compare the results of the two.
Isolate: remove the requirements and reintroduce them one at a time.
Rewrite the whole prompt from scratch with the four requirements.
items.r: Diagnosis by isolation: reintroducing them one at a time points to which of the three requirements breaks the result. Rewriting from scratch destroys the information about what failed, adding instructions on top of an overloaded prompt usually makes it worse, and switching model moves the wrong variable.

items.q: A workflow works but costs three manual iterations every time. Most effective optimisation?
o: Ask for three versions at once and keep the best one of them.
Use the most capable model available to skip the manual iterations.
Fix in the Project configuration whatever you always correct by hand.
Accept the three iterations as a normal, unavoidable cost of working with AI.
items.r: If you always correct the same thing, that correction is configuration, not work: moving it into the Project instructions makes it come out right first time. Accepting the cost optimises nothing, picking between three versions multiplies the review instead of reducing it, and a more capable model cannot guess preferences that are not written down.

items.q: A support agent can read tickets, draft replies, issue refunds and delete accounts. The team only needs read and draft. Applying least privilege, which change best reduces the risk?
o: Keep them active but with a prior confirmation by the operator.
Document in the system prompt that those tools must not be used.
Remove the refund and delete tools from the configuration.
Add logging to those tools to audit afterwards who used them.
items.r: Least privilege is removing the capability, not watching it: if the tool is not in the configuration, the failure is impossible. Logging is forensic and arrives once the refund has already gone out; confirmation depends on an attentive human and gives way to approval fatigue; an instruction in the prompt is not a control, it is a preference.

items.q: A RAG over technical documentation fails to retrieve chunks when the query contains exact identifiers like "error TS-999". What do you add?
o: Larger chunks, so the identifier ends up inside the context.
An embedding model with more dimensions and better resolution.
More results from the same vector index, raising the top-k.
BM25-style lexical search combined with the vector search.
items.r: Embeddings capture semantics and lose exact lexical matches: identifiers, error codes, rare proper nouns. BM25 recovers them, and combining both indexes via rank fusion is the recommended baseline. Bigger chunks, more dimensions or a higher top-k do not create a signal the vector index does not have.

items.q: Applying contextual retrieval over the baseline, which combination reduces retrieval failures the most?
o: Contextual embeddings + contextual BM25 + reranking.
Contextual embeddings only.
Reranking only, over the baseline.
Generic document summaries prepended to each chunk.
items.r: In the published data: contextual embeddings alone, −35% failures; adding contextual BM25, −49%; adding reranking, −67%. The benefits compound. Generic per-chunk summaries were one of the approaches Anthropic tested and discarded for very limited gains.

items.q: A stable knowledge base of around 300 pages feeds an internal assistant. Most reasonable retrieval architecture to start with?
o: Put it all in the prompt with prompt caching, no RAG.
A full RAG pipeline with vector DB, reranker and chunking.
Fine-tuning a model on those documents so that it memorises them.
A knowledge graph built out of those same documents.
items.r: The official guidance: if the base fits under ~200,000 tokens, load it whole and prompt caching cuts latency and cost drastically; measure, and add complexity only if the numbers demand it. Building RAG, fine-tuning or a graph over a stable corpus that fits in the window is unjustified complexity.

items.q: A system receives requests whose decomposition is not known in advance and varies case by case. Which pattern?
o: Orchestrator-workers: a central LLM decomposes and delegates.
Parallelization by sectioning, with the subtasks fixed in code.
Prompt chaining with a fixed sequence of verified steps.
Routing to one of three prompts specialised by request type.
items.r: The key difference between orchestrator-workers and parallelization is exactly that: in parallelization the subtasks are predefined in code; in orchestrator-workers the model determines them dynamically at runtime. Chaining and routing likewise presuppose a structure known in advance, which here does not exist.

items.q: There are clear evaluation criteria and the first outputs improve markedly when someone critiques them and they are regenerated. Which pattern fits?
o: Voting: generate N times in parallel and pick by majority.
Prompt chaining, adding more intermediate refinement steps.
Evaluator-optimizer: one generates and another scores the rubric.
Routing to a more capable model, which will get it right first time.
items.r: Evaluator-optimizer requires precisely the two conditions in the stem: articulable evaluation criteria and demonstrable improvement when feedback arrives; the loop generates, critiques against the rubric and iterates. Without clear criteria it spins without converging. Routing adds no critique, voting aggregates variants without evaluating them, and more chaining steps are not review.

items.q: A client asks for "a multi-agent system" to classify and answer high-volume, low-ambiguity incoming mail. What do you recommend?
o: Build the multi-agent system, which is exactly what the client asked for.
An autonomous agent with access to every mail tool available.
Fine-tuning your own model on the historical mail archive.
Start with a single optimised call with retrieval and examples.
items.r: Explicit recommendation: for many applications, optimising a single call with retrieval and in-context examples is enough, and complexity is added only if the metrics justify it. Multi-agent systems consume on the order of 15x the tokens of a chat and call for ambiguous, exploratory tasks; here volume is high and ambiguity low. A client naming an architecture does not make it the requirement.

items.q: The sponsor wants to know why the solution deserves investment. How do you frame it?
o: By the technical sophistication of the chosen architecture.
By the number of tools and agents that have been integrated.
By the model used: the most capable one is a quality argument.
Against measurable value pillars, with a current baseline.
items.r: Aligning the solution with business value pillars —operational efficiency, cost per case, performance against the SLA— is an objective of domain 1. Without a current baseline there is no way to demonstrate improvement, and architecture, tool count or model choice are means, not investment arguments for a sponsor.

items.q: You have time for 20 hand-graded cases or 200 with lower-nuance automated grading. What does the official guidance recommend?
o: Start with the 20 by hand and do not automate until they are stable.
Prioritise volume: the 200 with automated grading.
The 20 by hand: human judgement gives an irreplaceable signal.
Neither: use only qualitative evaluation on real traffic.
items.r: It is literal in the docs and counterintuitive, which is why it appears as an item: "More questions with slightly lower signal automated grading is better than fewer questions with high-quality human hand-graded evals". On human grading it says directly "avoid if possible", because it is slow and does not scale; and waiting for the 20 to stabilise defers coverage indefinitely.

items.q: You set up LLM-as-judge for summary quality. Which practices improve reliability? (select two)
o: Leave the rubric open, so the judge can add its own nuance.
A detailed rubric and a bounded output: binary or a 1-5 scale.
Ask it to reason before scoring and then discard that reasoning.
Use three different judges and average their scores to cancel bias.
items.r: The two reliable practices are the clear rubric with a bounded empirical output and prior reasoning that is then discarded. In Anthropic's research system, a single judge with a single call and one prompt proved more consistent than several averaged judges, which also multiply cost. And an open rubric destroys comparability across runs.

items.q: A system in production starts failing. Which diagnostic best distinguishes between prompt failure, hallucination and an inadequate model?
o: Increase the detail of the system prompt until the output improves.
Check the latency logs looking for the pattern of the failure.
Run the same input several times and observe the spread.
Move up to the most capable model and see if the failure goes away.
items.r: This is the best-of-N check: repeat the same request and look at the variance. Inconsistency across runs points to hallucination; systematic, reproducible failure points to the prompt or to model capability, and the two are separated with a case of known difficulty. Changing model or padding the prompt alters the system before you know what is broken, and latency says nothing about correctness.

items.q: Which grading method is preferable to check that an extraction returns exactly the correct identifier?
o: Code-based grading: exact comparison against what is expected.
LLM-as-judge scoring the output against a detailed rubric.
Human review by sampling over a batch of outputs.
Cosine similarity against the reference answer.
items.r: The official order of preference is code → LLM → human, for speed, cost and reliability. When correctness is binary and literal, exact comparison is the right instrument: the LLM is reserved for judgements with nuance, humans do not scale, and cosine similarity gives semantic closeness, which for an identifier is exactly what you do not want.

items.q: A healthcare client needs to process PHI. What is true about HIPAA enablement?
o: It is enabled per workspace and toggled depending on the workload.
Enabling zero data retention in the organisation is enough.
It is enabled per request through a parameter of the call.
It requires a signed BAA and applies at organisation level.
items.r: It is an organisation-level control and permanent: once enabled, not even an admin can disable it. That is why HIPAA and non-HIPAA workloads require separate organisations, not different workspaces nor a per-request flag. And with HIPAA active you do not additionally need ZDR.

items.q: Under a HIPAA agreement, where must PHI never appear?
o: In the content of the user messages of the conversation.
In the system prompt that configures the agent's behaviour.
In the JSON schema: property names and enum values.
In the tool_result blocks the tools return to the model.
items.r: Schemas —property names and enum, const or pattern values— are cached separately and do not receive the same protections as conversation content. Messages, system prompt and tool_result are covered by the agreement. It is a concrete rule, easy to break without noticing when modelling a field as an enum of real patient values.

items.q: An organisation with zero data retention wants to use the Batch API for an overnight workload. What do you warn them about?
o: That ZDR covers batch exactly like synchronous calls do.
That the API will block the request and return a 400 error.
That deleting the results manually at the end is enough.
The Batch API is not eligible for ZDR: it retains results.
items.r: Using batch under ZDR means opting out of the agreement for that data. A highly examinable distinction: under HIPAA the API blocks a non-eligible feature with a 400; under ZDR it does not block, that data simply falls outside the agreement, and deleting it afterwards does not bring it back in. Batch, Files API and code execution are not eligible.

items.q: A client asks for "an AI agent for customer service" with no further detail. First action as architect?
o: Propose a reference architecture with multi-agent and MCP.
Build a prototype this week to show something tangible.
Request access to their systems to assess technical feasibility.
Structured discovery of volume, success criteria and risk.
items.r: Discovery and requirements gathering is objective 6.1 and precedes everything else: volume, query types, existing systems, success criteria, error tolerance and who owns the risk. Without that agreed, any architecture is a bet, any prototype sets the wrong expectations, and technical access answers a question nobody has framed yet.

items.q: The client demands "99% accuracy" in a ticket-resolution agent. How do you handle it?
o: Accept the 99% and design the whole system to reach that figure.
Reject it: no LLM-based system ever reaches that accuracy.
Commit to 99% only on the easy cases and not measure the rest.
Turn it into a measurable metric and agree its threshold.
items.r: Managing expectations and SLAs is an objective of domain 6. "99% accuracy" means nothing without a definition of success or a case distribution. The work is turning it into a measurable metric on a real sample, showing the trade-off with cost and latency, and agreeing the threshold together with the escalation path for whatever falls outside. Accepting the figure as it stands commits to something you cannot verify; rejecting the project ignores that the threshold is negotiable; committing only on the easy cases leaves uncovered exactly where the system fails.

items.q: You are handing the system over to the client's internal team. What must the handoff include for it to survive six months?
o: The decisions with their why, the evals and the update procedure.
The source code and the credentials, which is what lets you run it.
An architecture diagram and a training session for the team.
The final prompts in a shared document everyone can edit.
items.r: What makes a system maintainable is the why behind each decision —with the alternatives that were rejected— and the ability to verify that a change does not break it. Without evals, the team cannot update the model without fear; without the rationale, it will undo deliberate decisions out of ignorance. Code and credentials let you operate it, not maintain it. A diagram and a training session expire with the first change, and loose prompts are the symptom, not the system.

items.q: An assistant over corporate documentation repeats an identical 30k-token preamble on every query. Most direct optimisation?
o: Prompt caching on that stable, repeated prefix.
Summarise the preamble to 3k tokens and accept the loss.
Switch to a model with a larger context window.
Split the preamble across several chained calls.
items.r: A large, stable, repeated prefix is the canonical caching case. The architectural key is discipline: you must keep constant the tools and the parameters that invalidate the prefix —changing the tool catalogue or the effort level between requests breaks it and you pay for a write every time. Summarising throws away information that is actually used; a larger window makes nothing cheaper because cost is per token processed; splitting multiplies the calls without removing the repetition.

items.q: A long-running agent accumulates bulky tool outputs that are no longer relevant. Context strategy?
o: Move all tool outputs to the system prompt, which is stable.
Prune the tool results that are no longer relevant.
Increase the max_tokens of the model's response.
Restart the session every ten turns to empty the context.
items.r: The official reasoning is direct: once a tool was called long ago, the agent does not need to see its raw result again, which is why tool result clearing is considered the lowest-risk compaction. max_tokens affects the output, not the accumulated input. Restarting every ten turns also throws away state the agent does need. And moving the outputs into the system prompt makes them permanent: it worsens exactly the problem you set out to solve.

items.q: You are debating whether to preload a repository's entire context or let the agent explore it at runtime. What does the official approach say?
o: It depends only on the total size of the repository on disk.
A hybrid: preload what is stable and retrieve the rest just-in-time.
Always preload everything that fits in the model's full context window.
Retrieve everything at runtime with tools, with nothing preloaded.
items.r: Claude Code is the hybrid example: CLAUDE.md, stable and high-signal, is loaded up front, and glob/grep retrieve just-in-time. The trade-off is explicitly acknowledged and accepted: runtime exploration is slower than precomputed retrieval. Filling the window with everything that fits dilutes the signal; retrieving absolutely everything at runtime pays latency even for what never changes; and the criterion is not repository size but which part is stable.

items.q: You want the whole team to share code conventions and MCP servers in a repo, with no manual per-person configuration. How?
o: A wiki document with the manual configuration steps.
Have each person configure it once in their user scope.
An onboarding script that writes each person's configuration.
CLAUDE.md and .mcp.json versioned in the project repo.
items.r: Configuring the environment for teams is domain 7: the project CLAUDE.md, the .mcp.json and the permission rules live in the project configuration, inside the repo. What lives in the repo is versioned, reviewed in a PR and arrives on its own; what depends on each person repeating steps —a wiki, the user scope, a script that writes local configuration— diverges within two weeks and nobody notices until something breaks.

items.q: A customer service assistant handles every incoming query with a single prompt: from "what are your opening hours?" to refund disputes with order history. The prompt loads 12 tools and some 4,000 words of policy in order to cover the worst case. Accuracy on the complex cases is good, but 70% of the volume is trivial queries that pay the same latency and the same cost. Which workflow pattern fits best?
o: Routing: a cheap classification step dispatches each query to a specialised prompt with its tools.
Keep the single prompt and move all traffic to a smaller model, accepting the loss of accuracy.
Parallelization: fire the full prompt and a reduced version at once and keep the first answer back.
Turn it into an autonomous agent that decides for itself how much policy to read on each query.
items.r: Routing. When queries fall into distinguishable categories and each category is better served by different handling, a cheap classification step lets you dispatch to a specialised prompt carrying only the tools that category needs: it separates concerns that, mixed into a single prompt, optimise poorly against each other. Dropping the model for all traffic sacrifices exactly the cases where it matters. Firing two versions in parallel doubles the cost and solves nothing. And making it an agent adds non-determinism to a problem whose routes are in fact known in advance.

items.q: A product description generator produces correct but flat text on the first pass. The team has explicit, written quality criteria — length, presence of specifications, tone, absence of empty superlatives — and a human reviewer identifies in seconds what is wrong with each text. The cost per description allows for several calls. Which pattern do you apply?
o: Raise the temperature to get more varied copy and then pick the best of them by hand each time.
Evaluator-optimizer: one generation call, a second that evaluates against the criteria, iterating.
A single longer prompt with the criteria and the instruction to "be critical of yourself first".
A multi-agent system with an agent dedicated to each one of the quality criteria.
items.r: Evaluator-optimizer. Its two applicability conditions are met: articulable evaluation criteria exist and critique produces a measurable improvement on the next iteration. One call generates, a second evaluates against the explicit criteria and returns actionable feedback, and it iterates until it passes or exhausts a cap on rounds. The loop separates generating from judging, which is what stops the model accepting its own output. Asking for self-critique within the same prompt does not separate the roles: the text is already written and the model tends to justify it. And one agent per criterion multiplies the cost without adding anything a single evaluator with the full rubric would not do.

items.q: A content classifier must detect an infrequent, high-impact category of violation. A single pass gives 91% accuracy but misses cases that, reviewed by hand, were clear. There are no subtasks to distribute: it is a single judgement on a single piece of content, and what is missing is confidence in that judgement. Which parallelization variant applies?
o: Orchestrator-workers: have a coordinator decide at runtime how many checks to fire.
Sectioning: split the content and evaluate each piece separately with the same prompt.
Parallelization does not apply: the judgement must be chained across several sequential steps.
Voting: run the same check with different framings and aggregate the results.
items.r: Voting. Parallelization has two variants and you choose between them by what is being parallelised. Sectioning distributes independent subtasks when the task divides naturally; voting repeats the same task with different approaches or framings and aggregates the results under an agreed decision rule, to gain confidence in a single result. Here there is nothing to distribute — it is one piece of content and one judgement — what is scarce is certainty. Splitting the content would also break the context that makes the violation recognisable.

items.q: A code migration assistant receives requests of the type "update all calls to the payments API v1 to use v2". Today it is implemented as parallelization with four fixed subtasks: models, services, tests and documentation. It fails repeatedly because in some repositories the changes touch six layers and in others only two, and which files are affected is not known until the code is inspected. Which pattern applies?
o: Stay on parallelization but expand to ten fixed subtasks to cover the large repositories too.
Routing: classify the repository by size and dispatch to a different subtask template per class.
Prompt chaining: chain the four subtasks in sequence instead of firing them at once.
Orchestrator-workers: a coordinator decides at runtime which subtasks are needed and delegates them.
items.r: The boundary between parallelization and orchestrator-workers is exactly this: whether the subtasks are predefined or the model decides them at runtime. Here they cannot be predefined because they depend on what is in each repository, so the coordinator inspects it first and delegates to a worker each subtask that is actually needed, which is precisely the signal for orchestrator-workers. Expanding to ten fixed subtasks carries the same defect with more waste. And classifying by size replaces real inspection with an approximation that does not predict which layers the change touches.

items.q: A financial analysis pipeline worked as a chain of prompts: extract figures from the report, compute ratios on those figures, compare the ratios against the sector and write the conclusion. It has been rewritten as a multi-agent system with one agent per step. Token consumption has gone up about 15x and result quality is the same or slightly worse. What is the explanation?
o: An evaluator agent is missing to review the others' output before the conclusion is issued.
The cost per agent is too high and the intermediate agents' model should be dropped.
The steps form a chain of dependencies, so there is nothing to run in parallel.
Agents need more warm-up turns and the system will improve as it accumulates run history.
items.r: Token spend is the argument that decides the architecture: an agent consumes on the order of 4x a chat and a multi-agent system around 15x, and that overhead is only amortised when the work splits into independent, simultaneous parallel pieces. Here each step needs the previous one's output, so there is nothing to split: you pay for each agent's context isolation and then pass it back what you already knew. The correct pattern for a linear dependency is prompt chaining.

items.q: An operations agent has tools to issue refunds, cancel subscriptions and close accounts. To control the risk, the team records every call with its parameters in an audited log and a manager reviews the log each morning. After a month there are three improper refunds already executed and detected the next day. Which design change fixes the underlying problem?
o: Introduce a human approval checkpoint before the irreversible tool executes, not after.
Strengthen the system prompt so the agent is extremely careful before issuing each refund.
Send an alert at the moment of execution so the manager can react to it immediately.
Extend the log to also capture the model's reasoning before each call, and review it twice a day.
items.r: A log is forensic, not preventive: however well built, it describes something that already happened. When a tool produces an irreversible effect, the human gate has to be wired into the loop before execution, so that without approval there is no call. Reviewing earlier, or more often, is still reviewing afterwards; an alert at the moment of execution stops nothing either. And an instruction to be careful is not a control: it reduces the frequency of the failure without bounding its consequence.

items.q: The finance team classifies invoices into six stable accounting categories, with written assignment rules and a result verifiable against the general ledger. It has been implemented as an agent with query tools and freedom to decide its own path. In production it gives different answers for the same invoice across runs, costs more than expected and the failures are hard to reproduce. What is the diagnosis?
o: More query tools are needed so the agent can check its decisions against the general ledger.
The agent needs few-shot examples of each accounting category in its system prompt.
The model temperature is too high for a deterministic classification task.
The steps can be written in advance: what applies is a workflow with predefined code paths.
items.r: The decision rule is whether you can write the exact steps in advance. Here you can: stable categories, written rules, verifiable output; the agent introduces non-determinism where it adds nothing. An agent is reserved for when you can give a goal and tools but not the path, and its price is exactly what is being suffered here: variability across runs and failures that are hard to reproduce. Few-shot examples and extra tools improve an agent that should not exist; lowering the temperature masks the symptom without removing the ability to choose the path.

items.q: To contain the cost of a long agentic loop, a developer sends only the system prompt and the last tool_result block on each request, instead of the full conversation. The agent starts repeating calls to tools it had already executed and loses decisions it took a few turns earlier. What is the cause?
o: The API is stateless: every request must carry the full history, with the previous pairs.
The maximum number of tool_use blocks allowed in one conversation has been exceeded.
The model's persistent memory between requests, which keeps past results, has not been enabled.
The max_tokens value is too low for the model to remember the earlier turns.
items.r: The agentic loop is maintained by the client, not the server: every request must resend the full message history, including the previous tool_use / tool_result pairs, because what is not resent the model does not have. Trimming the history erases the evidence of which tools were already executed, so the model requests them again, perfectly consistently with what it can see. max_tokens limits the output, not the input, and there is no implicit memory to fill the gap: if cost is a concern, you trim the content of the results, never the structure of the history.

items.q: A charge_card tool returned a network timeout error and the loop retried it, as configured. An audit finds duplicate charges: in several cases the charge had in fact completed at the payment provider and what was lost was the response. What fixes this in the design?
o: Extend the tool timeout until it stops firing at the latencies observed in production.
Remove automatic retry from all tools and escalate any failure to a human operator.
Return the failure as a tool_result with is_error: true so the model decides.
Give the operation an idempotency key and check whether it already completed before retrying.
items.r: A timeout is ambiguous by nature: it tells you no response arrived, not that nothing happened — it does not distinguish a failed call from a lost response. With irreversible effects that ambiguity has to be resolved in the tool layer — idempotency key or a prior state check — not delegated to the retry policy or the model's judgement. Marking is_error is correct so the agent can reason, but it does not prevent the second charge. And extending the timeout reduces the frequency of the scenario without eliminating it.

items.q: A diagnostic agent must locate the cause of an incident by reviewing fifteen large log files. After the review it finds the error, but from then on the rest of the conversation degrades: the agent answers imprecisely about things agreed before the review and context has to be repeated to it. Which architectural change avoids this?
o: Delegate the review to a subagent, whose context absorbs the raw volume and returns only the finding.
Compress the main conversation's context as soon as the review of the fifteen logs finishes.
Ask the agent for a summary of the logs at the end, so the files already read can be discarded.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so that the fifteen log files fit without degradation.
items.r: The main value of a subagent is not parallelism but context isolation: the dirty work happens in a window that is discarded and only the finding, with its evidence, returns to the parent. Summarising or compacting afterwards is too late, because the degradation already happened while the logs occupied the window. And a larger window does not avoid context rot: recall accuracy falls gradually as tokens accumulate, well before hitting the hard limit.

items.q: A coordinator fires four subagents in parallel to document four modules, and each must write its section into the same specification file. The result comes back incomplete in an irregular way: sometimes two sections are missing, sometimes only one, and not always the same ones. What fixes the design?
o: Raise each subagent's turn cap so that they all have time enough to finish writing their section.
Give each subagent an explicit instruction not to overwrite the others' work in the file.
Parallelise only reading and analysis, and have the coordinator compose and write the final file.
Fire the four subagents in sequence instead of in parallel, one after another.
items.r: Subagents work with isolated contexts and share no state: none sees what the others are doing, so concurrent writes to the same destination overwrite each other and the result depends on arrival order. Writing is a serialisation point and it belongs to the coordinator, which does have the full picture: each subagent returns its section and the coordinator composes the file. Instructing each subagent "not to overwrite" asks for coordination from something that lacks the information to coordinate. Serialising them would work, but it needlessly gives up the parallelism of the part that is genuinely independent: reading and analysing.

items.q: A contract reviewer receives a document of around 90 pages together with the question to answer. The prompt places the instruction first and then the full text of the contract. Quality is uneven: in some runs it cites the relevant clause well and in others it answers about a section that was beside the point. Which structural adjustment is most effective?
o: Put the long document first in the prompt and the question at the end, after the content.
Split the contract into two-page fragments and make one separate call for each fragment.
Repeat the instruction at the start and at the end of the prompt to reinforce it at both ends.
Wrap each clause in tags with its number so that the model is able to reference them.
items.r: With long inputs, order matters: the long content goes at the top and the question or instruction at the end, after the content, because that way the model reads the query with the whole document already present. It is one of the highest-effect, lowest-cost adjustments in long-context prompts. Splitting loses the cross-references, exactly what makes reviewing a whole contract useful. And tagging the structure helps, but does not correct the degradation caused by the order.

items.q: A support assistant holds conversations of twenty turns or more. The role, the tone and the hard prohibitions — never promise delivery dates, never quote prices without checking the catalogue — are repeated at the start of every user message so they are not forgotten. The cost per conversation grows with length and compliance still degrades in the final turns. What is the correction?
o: Reduce conversation length by cutting the cases into separate sessions of ten turns each.
Repeat the prohibitions at the end of each user message as well, to cover both ends of the turn.
Move role, tone and prohibitions to the system parameter, which governs the whole conversation.
Include the prohibitions as prefilled assistant blocks at the start of each turn.
items.r: Durable instructions — who the assistant is, in what tone and what it can never do — go in the system prompt, which governs the whole conversation without being reinjected into every message; the user turn is left with only the specific request. Repeating them turn by turn pays tokens for something the system parameter already guarantees and, diluted among conversational content, they lose the weight they carry as a system instruction. Cutting the conversations is not a prompt correction: it sacrifices the thread of the case to dodge the symptom.

items.q: An application assessment returns an object with two fields: decision, an enum of three values, and justification, free text. The JSON is always valid and decisions are issued without failure, but reviewers observe that the justification frequently seems written to defend the decision rather than to ground it, and that borderline decisions come out wrong. Which change fixes this?
o: Replace the enum with a numeric score that allows borderline cases to be nuanced.
Extend the justification field description to require citing the criteria applied.
Order the schema so the criteria analysis is generated before the decision field.
Make two separate calls, one for the decision and another one for the justification.
items.r: The model generates sequentially: what it emits earlier conditions what it emits later, and a decision field issued first cannot rest on later reasoning. With decision first, the justification is written after the fact on an already-fixed verdict — hence it sounds defensive — and the reasoning never gets to influence the decision, which is exactly where borderline cases are decided. Reversing the order turns the analysis field into prior reasoning. Hardening the field description does not change generation order, and splitting it into two calls leaves the second just as conditioned by the first.

items.q: Your team uses Claude to draft meeting summaries. Someone proposes measuring quality by asking the team every Friday whether they are "happy with the summaries". They have been answering yes for three months and, even so, two clients have complained about commitments the summary attributed to the wrong person. What is wrong with that way of measuring?
o: It should also ask the affected clients, not just the team that writes them.
The problem is the sample: very few of the team members reply each Friday.
It is not a measure: it defines no correct summary and is checked against nothing.
The frequency is insufficient; you would have to ask daily to catch the rare failures.
items.r: A useful success criterion is specific and measurable: "fewer than 2% of summaries attribute a commitment to the wrong person, measured over 100 sets of minutes with the correct attribution annotated by hand" can be checked; "are you happy?" cannot. Aggregate satisfaction hides exactly the rare, expensive failure. Asking more often, more people or the clients themselves measures the same thing with more noise: without defining what correct means, the specific failure that matters still never surfaces.

items.q: You are going to automate the classification of incoming emails into five categories. Before building anything, you want to know whether it will work. What is the first step?
o: Ask Claude to evaluate itself on a sample and report its own accuracy.
Start with the most capable model to maximise accuracy and measure later.
Build the full workflow and review the first week's results in production by hand.
Gather a set of emails already classified by hand, including the rare cases.
items.r: Having a good eval set is the most important step in the process, and it is what lets you measure before deploying. Without it there is no way to know whether a change improves or worsens things, nor to compare models. The set must resemble the real distribution of the task and include edge cases: ambiguous, empty, extremely long. Measuring in production is measuring with clients as guinea pigs, a self-evaluation without reference answers is not a measure, and picking a model before you can measure is picking blind.

items.q: You are evaluating an assistant that answers questions about internal policy. You can review 40 answers by hand very carefully, or generate 400 cases and score them automatically with a cruder criterion. The budget stretches to one of the two. Which do you choose?
o: The 40, and extrapolate the accuracy percentage to the rest of the volume.
The 40 reviewed by hand: human judgement makes up for the lower volume.
The 400 automatic ones: more coverage with a somewhat cruder signal.
Neither of the two: without 100% human review you cannot deploy.
items.r: The official recommendation is explicit: prioritise volume over the quality of the evaluation. More questions with an automated score of somewhat lower signal beats fewer questions judged by hand, because what you are after is detecting regressions and edge cases, and that shows up with coverage. Human evaluation is the most flexible and highest quality, but also the slowest and most expensive: it is avoided wherever it can be automated. Demanding full review stops you deploying anything, and extrapolating from 40 cases gives a useless interval.

items.q: The support assistant occasionally cites warranty clauses that do not exist in the policy document. The tone is confident and the formatting impeccable, so the agents do not spot it. Which technique attacks the problem at the root?
o: Extract the literal quotes from the document first and answer only from them.
Add an explicit "do not make up information" instruction to the prompt.
Review by hand each week a sample of the answers sent out to customers.
Lower the model's temperature so the answers come out more conservative and literal.
items.r: Grounding the answer in literal quotes extracted first forces the model to locate the text before reasoning over it, and leaves the evidence in plain sight so a human can check it in seconds. Temperature changes the style, not the fidelity to the document. A generic instruction not to make things up lowers the frequency without giving you a way to verify it. And reviewing a sample catches the failure afterwards, which is exactly what is not working here.

items.q: Two people on the team ask the assistant the same question in different words and get answers that contradict each other on the return deadline. Which success criterion describes what is failing?
o: Consistency: how similar the answers are for equivalent inputs.
Relevance: whether the answer really addresses what was asked.
Task fidelity: the accuracy measured over the held-out test set.
Context utilisation: how much it uses the information it is given.
items.r: Consistency is exactly that: if someone asks the same thing twice in different words, how much does it matter that they get semantically equivalent answers? It is a different criterion from accuracy —both answers can be plausible and one be wrong—, from context utilisation and from relevance: here both answers are relevant and use the context, yet they contradict each other. It is measured by comparing answers to paraphrases of the same question.

items.q: You want to score automatically whether the assistant's answers keep an empathetic tone with angry customers. Which scoring method fits?
o: Exact match against a reference answer written out in advance.
Searching for keywords such as "I understand" or "I am sorry".
A 1 to 5 scale judged by a model against a written rubric.
Human review of every answer, since it is a subjective judgement.
items.r: The method is chosen by the nature of the output. For closed categories, exact match; for nuanced judgements such as empathy or professionalism, a scale scored by a model with an explicit rubric, which defines what each level means and is fast, flexible and scalable. An empathetic tone matches no reference literally, and searching for keywords rewards the empty formula. Full human review does not scale: it is reserved for validating that the automated judge is reliable, and then the judge is scaled.

items.q: An invoice data extraction pilot has spent a month with 100% human review. Overall accuracy is 96% and the team wants to move to reviewing only a sample. What do you check before taking the step?
o: That the 96% holds up broken down by invoice type and by field.
That the monthly volume justifies the saving from dropping review.
That the model in use is the most capable available for the task.
That the overall accuracy still holds at 96% for one more week.
items.r: An aggregate average is where concentrated failures hide: an overall 96% can coexist with 60% on the invoices from one particular supplier or on the tax field, and another week of the same average would not reveal it. Before reducing oversight you have to break it down by segment and check that performance is consistent, not just high on average. Volume justifies the saving, but says nothing about the risk.

items.q: When defining the success criterion for a sentiment classifier, someone proposes "that the model classifies sentiment well". How do you reformulate it?
o: "That it gets it right in the great majority of cases it receives."
"That it matches or beats the accuracy of the team classifying today."
"That it reaches an F1 of at least 0.85 on a held-out message set."
"That no customer ever complains about a wrong classification."
items.r: A good criterion is specific, measurable, achievable and relevant: it names the metric, the set it is measured on, the threshold and where that threshold comes from —here, 10,000 diverse held-out messages and 5% above the current baseline. "That it gets it right in most cases" is not checkable; "that nobody complains" is neither achievable nor a measure of the task; and "that it matches the human team" is reasonable as a goal, but still does not say on what set or with what metric the comparison is made.

items.q: The team wants Claude to score another Claude's answers. What makes that scoring more reliable?
o: Using the same system prompt both to generate and to score, for coherence.
Giving a detailed rubric, reasoning before the mark, bounded output.
Asking it to score from 0 to 100 to get more resolution in the mark.
Having it score the answer several times and keeping the highest mark.
items.r: Three things raise the judge's reliability: a concrete rubric, reasoning before scoring —and discarding that reasoning— and a bounded, empirical output, of the "correct/incorrect" kind or a number from a short range. A 0 to 100 scale gives false precision and scores that cannot be compared across runs. Keeping the highest mark turns the evaluation into advertising. And the model doing the judging had better not carry over the prompt or the context of the one that generated.

items.q: The operations team processes 4,000 refund requests a month following a written seven-step procedure, always the same, with an outcome checkable against the billing system. How do you design it?
o: As a workflow with predefined steps, the model only on the language ones.
As an autonomous agent with access to the billing system in each case.
As a conversational assistant guiding an expert human operator step by step.
As an agent with a human who approves each one of the seven steps.
items.r: The decision rule is whether you can write the exact steps in advance. Here you can: written procedure, always the same, verifiable outcome, and the rest of the work is code. A workflow gives predictability and consistency, and costs less. An agent is reserved for when you know how to give a goal and tools but not the path; here it would only add variability between runs and failures that are hard to reproduce. And guiding or approving 4,000 cases a month by hand automates nothing.

items.q: A director wants to "put AI into" the client onboarding process because the board has asked for it. When you ask which part hurts, nobody can say: the process takes eleven days and there is no measurement of which step the time goes on. What do you propose first?
o: Train the team so they spot the opportunities themselves.
A pilot on the most visible use case, to demonstrate value fast.
Measure where the time goes and how often each step fails.
Automate the most manual step, usually the costliest one.
items.r: Baseline first, decision about what to automate second. Without a measure you can neither choose the right step nor demonstrate afterwards that anything has improved. The most manual step is not necessarily the slowest nor the most expensive in errors. A pilot chosen for visibility optimises for the board's photo, not for the process, and leaves the team with no way to defend the next investment with data. Training without a diagnosis delegates the diagnosis to whoever has the least data.

items.q: A contract review workflow produces a draft risk summary that a lawyer then signs off. To go faster, the team proposes that contracts below €5,000 be approved without human review. What do you consider?
o: That the threshold should be set by the cost of being wrong, not by the value.
That the threshold is reasonable because it caps exposure at the contract value.
That no contract should be approved without human review, whatever the value.
That the threshold should be based on the confidence the model itself declares.
items.r: An unlimited liability clause in a small contract is not a small risk. The human gate goes where an error is hard to reverse, and that does not correlate with the value: an indemnity or an exclusivity in a minor contract can cost far more than the contract, so capping exposure at the signed amount is an accounting illusion. Reviewing everything indiscriminately is not a criterion either, it is the absence of one. And the model's self-declared confidence is not calibrated by default: it is useful if you validate it against labelled data, not before.

items.q: You are deciding whether a use case is a good candidate for Claude. Which of these signals most argues against starting there?
o: The task requires reading very long documents, hundreds of pages.
The volume is high and the budget per query is fairly tight.
The output must follow a strict format that another system consumes.
There is no agreed criterion for recognising a correct output.
items.r: If nobody can say whether a given output is correct —not even on manual review—, there is no way to evaluate, to improve, or to know when you have finished: the project has no completion criterion. The other three are design constraints with known solutions —long context, model choice and cost, structured output— not blockers to starting.

items.q: In a customer service workflow, the assistant answers 80% of queries well and the remaining 20% need a person. Which part of the design is most important to get right?
o: The model chosen, so as to maximise first-contact resolution.
The response time, so that the customer perceives no waiting.
The wording of the answers for the 80%, which is the bulk of the daily volume.
The criterion for when to escalate, with explicit examples of both sides.
items.r: The expensive one is neither the query resolved well nor the one escalated well: it is the one resolved on its own when it should have been escalated. The escalation criterion is the boundary of the system and it is best written with cases that are resolved and cases that are handed over, not left to inference. Improving the wording of the 80% polishes what already works; moving up a model shifts the percentage but does not define the boundary; and response time does not change who decides what.

items.q: The marketing team wants the assistant to draft posts and publish them straight to the company's social media with no intervention. What do you answer?
o: That it is viable if a banned-words filter is added before publishing.
That it is viable if all posts are logged so they can be audited later.
That it is not viable with any design, since generated text is never quite reliable.
That publishing is public and irreversible, so a person takes the last step.
items.r: The criterion is not the quality of the text but the reversibility of the action. A social media post spreads and is captured in seconds: deleting it afterwards does not undo the damage. A log is forensic, not preventive, and a banned-words list does not capture the real problem, which is one of fit and context. Discarding the whole case is not right either: with the person at the last step, the workflow still saves almost all the work.

items.q: A process has three chained stages: extract data from a document, check it against the ERP and draft a notification. Each stage depends on the previous one. Someone proposes building it as three agents working in parallel. What do you point out?
o: That it is correct because each stage is a separate responsibility.
That even more agents are needed, one for each type of document.
That the stages are chained dependencies: there is nothing to parallelise.
That the parallelism will work if each agent waits for the previous one to finish.
items.r: The right move is to chain the steps, and the extra cost of multi-agent buys nothing here. Separating responsibilities and running them in parallel are different things: a multi-agent system is paid for with considerably higher consumption, and that only pays off when the subtasks are independent and simultaneous. Adding agents per document type multiplies the cost without breaking the dependency. A strict chain is designed as a chain: each step receives the output of the previous one, with the added benefit that you can validate between steps.

items.q: An HR team wants to use Claude to score candidates and automatically reject those who do not reach a threshold. What is the most important objection?
o: That the model might not have been trained on CVs from this particular sector.
That the candidates' names would need to be anonymised before sending them.
That the cost per application would be too high in high-volume, low-conversion campaigns.
That automatically rejecting a person's access to employment demands human oversight.
items.r: Automatic rejection in recruitment is a high-impact decision about a person: it demands human intervention and traceability of the reason, not an opaque threshold. Anonymising reduces one specific bias and is good practice, but it does not make the decision appropriate to automate. Cost per application and the model's command of the domain are implementation considerations: they are solved with budget or with examples, and they change nothing about who answers for the rejection.

items.q: Someone on the team pastes the full payroll listing into the assistant to ask for a summary of the wage bill by department. What is the relevant point?
o: That the summary will come out imprecise because there are too many rows to aggregate.
That personal data should only go in if the processing is foreseen and authorised.
That the file would need splitting into several parts to stay under the limit.
That it is worth explicitly asking it not to memorise that information.
items.r: The criterion is set by the company's data policy, not by the convenience of the task. The right question is not whether it technically fits, but whether that processing is foreseen and authorised. Identifiable pay data has its own rules in almost any organisation, and the alternative is usually trivial: aggregate before sending, which also gives a better result and removes the length problem along the way. Asking the model "not to memorise" is not a control: controls live in the contract, the configuration and the process.

items.q: An internal legal queries assistant answers a question about a procedural deadline confidently and gets it wrong. The lawyer who used it did not check because "it had been getting things right for weeks". What is failing in the governance of the system?
o: A more restrictive prompt was missing to limit the scope of the answers.
A visible warning that the output needs checking, plus a process enforcing it.
The assistant should have cited the statutory source for its answer.
The model chosen is not capable enough for the legal domain and its procedural deadlines.
items.r: Two linked things: communicating visibly that the output requires verification, and a process that makes it mandatory wherever there are consequences. The risk here is not a one-off error —that is taken for granted— but the accumulated confidence that means nobody checks. A more restrictive prompt narrows the scope, not the user's belief. Citing the source helps a great deal, but it is part of that verification, not a substitute: an unchecked citation is another piece of data to be believed.

items.q: Management asks what happens to the information the team writes in conversations with Claude. What is the responsible answer?
o: That it is enough not to type confidential information into the conversations.
That the data never leaves the organisation, under any product or plan.
That it depends on the product and the contract: check the current terms.
That all data is used for training unless that option is switched off in settings.
items.r: The conditions for processing, retention and use for training depend on the product, the plan and the contract, and they change. Asserting from memory in either direction —"it never leaves" or "everything is used unless you switch it off"— is exactly the kind of answer that creates a compliance problem. And leaving each person to decide what counts as confidential is not a policy, it is luck. The professional answer is to point to where it is written and check it for the organisation's specific contract and configuration.

items.q: You are evaluating two proposed uses: (a) generating draft replies to customer reviews, which a community manager checks; (b) generating fictitious positive reviews to publish as if they came from customers. How do you treat them?
o: The first is normal use with review; the second deceives by design.
Both require a visible notice that the content is AI-generated.
The second is acceptable if the reviews describe real features.
Both are acceptable if a manager reviews them before they are published.
items.r: Human review does not fix the second case. The difference is not quality or oversight, but whether the content deceives about its origin. A draft that a professional reviews and signs off on is assisted work. A fictitious review presented as a customer's experience is fraudulent even if every claim about the product is true, and reviewing it better only makes it more convincing. Labelling it as generated does not save it either: it would still be an invented testimonial.

items.q: A manager wants to roll the assistant out to 400 people next week. What is the minimum that must exist first?
o: A service level agreement with guaranteed response times for users.
A dashboard of usage metrics per person and per team, reviewed every week.
Compulsory in-person training for all 400 people in the rollout.
A guide to valid uses, what not to type, and where to report failures.
items.r: The minimum viable governance is that people know which uses are appropriate, what they must not type in and who to alert, and that there is a channel by which failures get back to whoever can fix them. Without that loop, problems turn into corridor folklore. Training helps but ages; a service level agreement governs availability, not use; and usage metrics per person measure activity, not value or risk.

items.q: You ask for summaries of sales calls and the format changes on every run: sometimes bullets, sometimes paragraphs, sometimes with different sections. What is most effective?
o: Repeat in the prompt that the format must always be the same.
Include two or three complete input and output examples.
Ask for the output as a single paragraph to reduce variability.
Run it several times and keep the one with the best format.
items.r: Examples in the exact format you want, complete input and output: it is the most direct way to pin down format and tone, because they teach what an abstract description cannot convey, and they settle the edge cases too if you choose them well. Insisting on the instruction gives the model no pattern to copy. Flattening the output into one paragraph removes the variation by removing the structure that was useful to you. And hand-picking the best run is not a method, it is manual quality control repeated on every call.

items.q: You have to analyse an 80-page report and answer five questions about it. How do you structure the request?
o: A summary of the document first, and the questions about it.
The document first and the questions after the content.
The questions first, so it knows what to look for while reading.
One request per question, sending the whole document each time.
items.r: With long inputs, the content goes at the top and the query at the end. It is one of the highest-impact, lowest-cost adjustments in long context, and the reverse order is precisely the one that loses the effect. Asking about a summary loses the detail the full report was there for. And one call per question multiplies the cost without improving anything when all five fit in the same request.

items.q: A colleague writes very long prompts with plenty of company context and still gets generic answers. On inspection, the prompt describes the situation in detail but never says exactly what they want back. What do you suggest?
o: State explicitly what output they want, for whom and what it must contain.
Split the prompt across several shorter, more focused conversations.
Use a more capable model, which will infer the author's intent better.
Trim the context, because so much company detail ends up diluting the request.
items.r: That is exactly what is missing from their prompt. Abundant context and a vague request produce generic answers: the model has plenty to talk about and no instruction on what to deliver. The fix is to name the output: which artefact, for which audience, with which parts and at what length. The context is not excessive, and splitting it across conversations only spreads the same ambiguity. A better model infers better, but it is still guessing the brief.

items.q: You want the assistant to keep the same role, tone and prohibitions throughout a long conversation with many turns. Where do you put those instructions?
o: At the end of the conversation, before the important request.
At the start of the first message, which carries the most weight.
Repeated at the start of every message, so they do not get diluted.
In the system or project instructions for the space.
items.r: Lasting instructions —who it is, in what tone and what it must never do— go in the system or project configuration: they govern every turn without anyone re-injecting them by hand. Repeating them in every message pays for the same text over and over and, mixed in with conversational content, they lose the weight they carry as a system instruction. Putting them only at the start or only at the end leaves them at the mercy of recall degradation in a long conversation.

items.q: You ask Claude to decide whether an incident is critical and to justify the decision. The justifications read like a defence of a decision already taken, and it seldom gets the borderline cases right. What do you change?
o: Require the justification to cite the specific criteria applied.
Make two separate requests: one for the verdict, one to justify it.
Ask it to set out its reasoning before the verdict, not after.
Ask for a numeric score instead of a category, easier to calibrate.
items.r: The model generates sequentially: what it emits earlier conditions what comes later. With the verdict first, the justification is written on top of a decision already fixed —hence the defensive tone— and the reasoning never gets to influence where it is most needed, which is the borderline cases. Reversing the order turns the analysis into reasoning that comes first, and there it can still change the verdict. Swapping the category for a number does not move the order: the figure still comes out before the analysis. Requiring cited criteria improves the shape of the justification, not the decision. And splitting it into two requests leaves the second just as conditioned by the first.

items.q: You are going to classify 200,000 support messages a month into five simple categories, with tight latency and a contained budget. Where do you start?
o: With two models in parallel, comparing results for a month.
With the mid-tier model, a safe middle ground on cost and quality.
With the most capable model, to secure accuracy from day one.
With a fast, cheap model, measuring whether it meets the requirements.
items.r: For high volume and a narrow task, the recommended approach is to start with efficiency: implement with a fast, cheap model, test the use case thoroughly and move up only if a specific shortfall appears. It lets you iterate fast and cheaply. Starting with the most capable one leaves you not knowing whether you needed it, and pays the top rate on 200,000 messages a month. Running two models in parallel for a month doubles the cost to answer a question a handful of evals settle in a day. And defaulting to the middle is choosing without measuring.

items.q: A complex reasoning task on regulation fails with the current model on the hard cases. Before switching models, which lever is worth considering?
o: Run the query several times and compare answers.
Split the regulation into fragments and query each one.
Lengthen the prompt with more regulatory context.
Adjust the effort level within the same model.
items.r: Several models support an effort parameter that trades intelligence against latency and cost without leaving the model. Adjusting it is often a better lever than jumping to another model, and it is reversible and measurable. Only if the evals still fall short at high effort does moving to a more capable model make sense. Adding more regulation to the prompt does not buy reasoning capacity: the hard cases fail on reasoning, not on missing text. Running it several times only reveals the variability. And splitting the regulation blocks exactly the cross-cutting reasoning those cases demand.

items.q: After two months in production, someone proposes dropping to a cheaper model to reduce cost. How do you decide?
o: Try the cheap model in production for a week and see if anyone complains.
Compare both models on your eval set, with your prompts and data.
Consult the model's published comparisons and decide with those.
Keep the current one: moving down always degrades quality.
items.r: The decision to switch models is taken with your eval set, your prompts and your real data, comparing accuracy, quality and edge-case handling against the saving. Public comparisons measure other tasks with other prompts; they are useful for ruling out, not for deciding. Testing in production turns your users into the test set, and "nobody complained" is not a measurement: silent failures generate no complaints. And refusing on principle gives up a saving that is often real with no measurable loss.

items.q: A workflow has a great many simple decisions and a few genuinely hard ones. The budget does not stretch to resolving everything with the most capable model. What do you propose?
o: Combine models: a cheap one for the bulk, the capable one for the hard cases.
Process only the hard decisions and leave the simple ones unautomated.
Reduce the volume by filtering with deterministic rules first.
Resolve everything with the mid-tier model and accept the loss on the hard ones.
items.r: Multi-model strategies exist for this: a cheap executor that escalates the hard decisions to a more capable adviser, or an orchestrator that delegates the bulk work to cheap workers. That way most tokens are billed at the low rate and capability is reserved where it changes the outcome. Using the mid-tier for everything overpays on the simple ones and still fails on the hard ones. Automating only the hard ones throws away the saving where the volume is. And filtering with rules is compatible and helps, but on its own it does not resolve the hard ones.

items.q: Five people on the team each write their own prompt for drafting sales proposals. The results vary widely in structure and tone, and each person maintains their own. What fixes this sustainably?
o: Train the team in advanced prompting techniques.
Each person saves their favourite prompt and reuses it.
A shared space with the common instructions and reference documents.
Circulate by email the prompt of whoever gets the best results.
items.r: Shared configuration —instructions and reference material in a single place— means an improvement reaches everyone at once and the knowledge outlives whoever leaves. Five copies diverge the moment someone improves theirs: it is the same problem as having five versions of a template. Circulating a prompt by email creates the sixth copy, and a week later everyone has their own tweaked version. Training the team improves the people, but the variation returns as soon as someone new joins, because the problem is not skill but where the configuration lives.

items.q: You have loaded twenty reference documents into a shared space and the answers have got worse: it mixes old policies with current ones. What do you do?
o: Ask it in the instructions to prioritise the most recent documents.
Rename the files putting the effective date in the name.
Add more documents so that it has the complete context.
Remove what is obsolete and keep only the current version of each policy.
items.r: A knowledge space is not a historical archive: every contradictory document is a chance to answer wrongly, and the model has no reliable way of knowing which one rules. The fix is to curate the material and leave a single current version. Adding more documents makes worse exactly what is failing. Putting the date in the name or asking it to prioritise the recent ones are patches that depend on the model correctly interpreting metadata you could have deleted: the day it slips, the old policy comes back out as if it were still in force.

items.q: Your assistant must always answer in the brand tone and never promise delivery dates. Where does that rule live?
o: In an internal note the team consults before writing.
In the instructions of the shared configuration for the space.
In the first message of each conversation, written by the person.
In the model's own memory, which remembers it between conversations.
items.r: Permanent rules live in the configuration, which applies to every conversation in that space without anyone having to remember. Not in people's discipline nor in an implicit memory that does not exist between conversations. An internal note you have to remember to read gets skipped the day someone is in a hurry, which is exactly when a deadline gets promised that cannot be met. And typing it by hand in each conversation is the same rule resting on the same human memory, only paying for the text every time.

items.q: A colleague suggests dumping the entire employee handbook, 300 pages, into the shared configuration "just in case". What do you reply?
o: That the handbook will not fit whole and has to be split by chapter.
That it has to be converted to plain text before loading it.
That it is a good idea: the more context, the better the answers.
That useful context is selected, not accumulated just in case.
items.r: More context is not better context. Irrelevant material competes for the model's attention with what does matter, in large sets retrieval accuracy falls, and it makes every request more expensive. The right question is which questions this space has to answer and which documents are needed for that; the rest stays where it was, a search away. Splitting it up or converting it to plain text are format questions: they settle how the handbook goes in, not whether it should.
